questions.stem: Shape factor of rolled beam lies between:
questions.solution:
**1.10 to 1.20.**

Shape factor is the ratio of plastic to elastic moment capacity, and depends only on the shape of the section:

> f = M_{p}/M_{y} = (f_{y}Z_{p})/(f_{y}Z_{e}) = Z_{p}/Z_{e}

For a standard rolled I-beam most of the area is already in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, so there is little reserve between first yield and full plasticity — hence a low shape factor of about **1.10–1.20**.

Values worth memorising:

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **Rolled I-beam** | **1.10 – 1.20** |
| I-section (general) | 1.2 – 1.4 |
| Rectangle | 1.5 |
| Circle | 1.7 |
| Triangle | 2.34 |
| Diamond | 2.0 |

examTip.trick: Shape factor **S = Z_p/Z_e** measures the reserve between first yield and full plasticity. Learn the ladder: **rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, diamond 2.0, I-section (rolled beam) 1.10–1.20.**
examTip.mnemonic: **An I-section has the LOWEST shape factor** — because its material is already concentrated in the flanges, so there is little left to yield after the extreme fibre goes. A rectangle has plenty of under-worked material near the neutral axis, hence 1.5.

questions.stem: Water may not contain much impurities if its source is:
questions.solution:
**Spring along hill slopes.**

A hill-slope spring discharges **groundwater** that has already been filtered through the soil profile, and it rises in sparsely populated, largely non-agricultural terrain. So both the pollutant load and the organic content are low.

Why the others carry more impurity:
- **Reservoirs and lowland lakes** — water stagnates, nutrients accumulate and algal growth follows.
- **Streams in plains** — receive industrial effluent and agricultural run-off carrying fertiliser and pesticide.

One caveat the examination likes: a **hot spring** is an exception, because it usually carries dissolved sulphur and is generally unsuitable for supply.

examTip.trick: Rank sources by natural filtration: **spring water** has percolated through soil and rock, which removes most turbidity and bacteria. Surface sources (river, lake, pond) have had no such treatment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ground filters, surface does not.** But spring water is not automatically safe — it can carry dissolved minerals and can be contaminated near the outlet, so it is still tested and usually disinfected.

questions.stem: Critical hydraulic gradient is formed if:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — the three statements describe one condition from three angles.

The critical hydraulic gradient is reached when upward seepage force exactly balances the buoyant weight of the soil skeleton:

> i_{cr} = (G_{s} − 1)/(1 + e)

which for typical values (G_{s} ≈ 2.65, e ≈ 0.65) gives i_{cr} ≈ **1.0**.

At that instant:
- the **flow/seepage must be upward** (a downward gradient only adds to effective stress);
- the **effective stress becomes zero**, σ′ = σ − u = 0;
- the soil loses all shear strength, since τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ → 0 for sand.

This is the **quick sand** or **boiling** condition, and it is why upward seepage at the downstream toe of a dam or inside an excavation is so dangerous.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" is correct here, but candidates often stop at the first plausible option. Read every alternative before committing on this question type.
examTip.trick: The critical condition can be stated three equivalent ways — **σ′ = 0**, **i = i_c**, and the seepage force equalling the submerged weight. All describe the same instant.
examTip.mnemonic: **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.** Design with a factor of **4 to 7**, high because piping is sudden, progressive and gives no warning.

questions.stem: For a saddle siphon, the maximum operative head is 4.53 m. The width and height of the throat of the siphon are 5 m and 2.25 m respectively. The coefficient of discharge is 0.90. How many units are required to pass a flood of 350 cumecs?
questions.solution:
**Four units.**

A siphon spillway runs full, so it behaves as an orifice:

> Q = C_{d} · A · √(2gH)

**Throat area:**
> A = 5 × 2.25 = 11.25 m²

**Discharge per unit:**
> Q = 0.90 × 11.25 × √(2 × 9.81 × 4.53)
> Q = 0.90 × 11.25 × √88.88
> Q = 0.90 × 11.25 × 9.428 = **95.46 m³/s**

**Number of units:**
> n = 350 / 95.46 = 3.67

A fraction of a siphon is meaningless and rounding down would leave the flood un-passed, so round **up: 4 units.**

Note the trap — 3.67 tempts option (c). Capacity questions always round up.

examTip.trick: The **operative head** is the head available to drive the siphon, and the throat is sized so the flow passes without the pressure dropping to vapour pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **A saddle siphon primes itself when the reservoir rises above the hood, runs FULL BORE, and de-primes as the level falls.** No moving parts and no operator — but it is vulnerable to **debris blocking the hood**, which is why trash screens are essential.

questions.stem: The maximum bending moment due to a train of wheel loads on a simply supported girder:
options: Always occurs at the centre of span
Always occurs under a wheel load
Never occurs under a wheel load
questions.solution:
**Always occurs under a wheel load.**

For a moving train of concentrated loads the bending moment diagram is made of straight segments, with a change of slope only where a load sits. A maximum of such a piecewise-linear function can therefore only occur **at one of those break points** — that is, under a wheel.

The governing criterion is that the maximum moment occurs under the load for which the ratio of the load on the left of it to the total load is closest to a/L (the section position ratio) — checked load by load.

Why the others fail:
- **Centre of span** is only true for a single point load or a symmetric UDL, not a train.
- **Never under a wheel load** is the exact opposite of the truth.

Contrast: for a **UDL longer than the span**, the maximum moment does occur at mid-span.

examTip.trap: "At midspan" is the reflex answer, true only for a **single** load. For a **train** of loads the maximum occurs under one of the wheels — but generally **not** at midspan.
examTip.trick: The governing rule: the absolute maximum moment occurs **under the load nearest the resultant**, when **midspan bisects the distance between that load and the resultant of all loads on the span**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always under a wheel, rarely at midspan.** Because the moment diagram for a set of point loads is made of straight segments, its peak must sit at a vertex — that is, under a load.

questions.stem: Strain energy in a simply supported beam loaded with point load W at the centre is:
questions.solution:
**W²l³/96EI.**

Central deflection of a simply supported beam with a central point load:

> δ = Wl³/(48EI)

For a linearly elastic system the load builds up from zero to W, so the work done — and hence the stored strain energy — is **half** the product of load and deflection:

> U = ½ · W · δ
> U = ½ · W · Wl³/(48EI)
> U = **W²l³/(96EI)**

Two checks that kill the wrong options instantly:
- Energy must be **quadratic in W**, so any option linear in W (a, b, d) cannot be right.
- Energy has units of force × length; W²l³/EI does, and Wl²/EI does not.

examTip.trick: Strain energy is the **work done by the load**: **U = ½Wδ**, and for a central point load **δ = Wl³/48EI**. So U = ½ × W × Wl³/48EI = **W²l³/96EI** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **U = ½Wδ — derive it rather than memorise it.** The same route works for any standard case: get the deflection, halve the product. From here **Castigliano** gives δ = ∂U/∂W, which returns Wl³/48EI ✓ — a neat self-check.

questions.stem: Correct relation between shear force S and bending moment M is:
questions.solution:
**S = dM/dx.**

From equilibrium of an elemental length dx of a loaded beam:

> dM/dx = S   (shear force is the slope of the bending moment diagram)
> dS/dx = −w  (load intensity is the negative slope of the shear force diagram)

The practical consequences are what get examined:
- Where **S = 0**, the BM diagram has zero slope — so **maximum bending moment occurs where shear force changes sign**.
- A **UDL** gives a linear SF diagram and a **parabolic** BM diagram.
- A **point load** gives a step in SF and a kink in BM.

Option (b) inverts the relation; (c) and (d) are dimensionally meaningless.

examTip.trick: Differentiate the moment and you get the shear. Check by degree: a UDL gives a **linear** shear and a **parabolic** moment — the moment is one degree higher, which is what integration does.
examTip.mnemonic: **w → V → M by successive integration; M → V → w by differentiation.** Hence **V = 0 marks a moment peak**, and the **change in M equals the AREA of the shear diagram** — the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the use of altitude valves?
options: To allow water to flow in one direction only
To blow off or remove the sand
Distribution system to shut off the supply whenever required
Supplies water to elevated tanks or standpipes
questions.solution:
**Supplies water to elevated tanks or standpipes** — and, more precisely, it stops them overflowing.

An altitude valve is fitted on the inlet line of an elevated service reservoir or standpipe. It stays open while the pressure on the pump side exceeds the tank side, so the tank fills; once the tank reaches its set level the valve closes automatically, preventing overflow, and it reopens to let the tank feed the network when demand draws the pressure down.

Match the other options to their own valves:

| Function | Valve |
|---|---|
| Flow in one direction only | **Reflux / check (non-return) valve** |
| Remove settled sand and silt | **Scour / blow-off valve** |
| Shut off supply at will | **Sluice / gate valve** |
| Release trapped air | Air relief valve |
| Control pressure | Pressure reducing valve |

examTip.trick: An altitude valve closes automatically when the tank reaches a set level, preventing overflow, and reopens as the level drops. It is a **level control**, not a pressure or flow device.
examTip.mnemonic: **Altitude valve watches the ALTITUDE of the water in the tank.** The name gives the function away.

questions.stem: When did the Government of Nepal form the Nepal Engineering Council?
questions.solution:
**2055 BS.**

The Nepal Engineering Council was established under the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**, and came into being on **11 March 1999**, which falls in 2055 BS.

What NEC does, and is asked about:
- Registers engineers and maintains the register of engineering professionals.
- Conducts the **registration (license) examination** — the examination this syllabus belongs to.
- Recognises engineering qualifications and accredits programmes.
- Regulates professional conduct and can take disciplinary action.

Do not confuse it with the **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)**, which is a professional membership body, not the statutory regulator.

examTip.trick: The Nepal Engineering Council Act is **2055 BS (1998 AD)**, and the Council itself was constituted the same year.
examTip.mnemonic: **Act 2055, Regulations 2057.** Worth also holding: the Council has a chairman and vice-chairman nominated by the Government (needing 15 and 10 years' experience), five government nominees, and **two engineers nominated by the Council itself**.

questions.stem: For the same power output, which power plant of the following has minimum operating charges?
questions.solution:
**Hydropower plant.**

Split the cost into two parts and the answer is immediate:

| Plant | Initial cost | Fuel cost | Operating cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hydropower** | **Very high** (dam, tunnel, powerhouse) | **Zero** | **Lowest** |
| Nuclear | Highest | Low but non-zero | Low–moderate |
| Thermal (coal) | Moderate | High | High |
| Gas turbine | Lowest | Highest | Highest |

Hydropower has **no fuel cost at all** — water arrives free — and needs little manpower and maintenance once commissioned. Its penalty is the enormous capital cost and long construction period, not its running cost.

That combination is exactly why hydropower is used for **base load** while gas turbines, cheap to build but expensive to run, are kept for **peak load**.

examTip.trick: Compare what each plant must **buy** to run: thermal needs coal, diesel needs fuel, nuclear needs enriched fuel and heavy safety staffing. **Hydropower's fuel is free** — the operating cost is essentially maintenance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydro: highest capital cost, lowest running cost, longest life.** That inversion is exactly why it suits Nepal, and why the economics turn on the discount rate and the construction period rather than on fuel prices.

questions.stem: Power needed to uplift water can be calculated as:
questions.solution:
**P = γQH** (with efficiency, P = ηγQH).

Derive it rather than memorise it. Weight of water lifted per second is γQ, and each unit weight is raised through head H, so

> Power = (weight per second) × (height) = **γQH**

**Dimensional check** — the fastest way to eliminate the distractors:
> γ [N/m³] × Q [m³/s] × H [m] = N·m/s = **watt** ✓

Option (a) uses area instead of discharge, giving N·m²/m³·... which is not power; (c) and (d) divide by H and fail dimensionally as well.

In practice:
> P = γQH/η for a **pump** (input power is larger)
> P = ηγQH for a **turbine** (output power is smaller)

with γ = 9810 N/m³ for water.

examTip.trick: **P = γQH** in watts, with γ in N/m³, Q in m³/s and H in m. Dimension check: (N/m³)(m³/s)(m) = N·m/s = watts ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **P ≈ 9.81 Q H kW**, and multiply by the efficiency (0.7–0.85 for a small scheme) for the real output. For a **pump** you divide by the efficiency instead of multiplying — the same formula, the other way round.

questions.stem: Which is the binding material used in road pavement?
questions.solution:
**Bitumen.**

In a flexible pavement bitumen is the binder: a semi-solid petroleum residue that coats the aggregate and glues the particles into a coherent, slightly flexible mass — asphalt concrete. It also waterproofs the layer.

Why not the others:
- **Stone dust** is a filler, occupying voids; it binds nothing.
- **Cement** is the binder in a **rigid** pavement (plain cement concrete), not in the bituminous surfacing the question implies.
- **Lime** is used to **stabilise** a subgrade, not to bind a pavement surface.

The distinction to carry forward: **flexible pavement → bituminous binder, load spread through the layers to the subgrade; rigid pavement → cement concrete slab, load carried by slab flexural strength.**

examTip.trick: The pavement layers each have a job: **bitumen binds** the aggregate in a flexible pavement; the aggregate carries the load; the subgrade supports everything.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bitumen for flexible pavements, cement for rigid ones.** A flexible pavement spreads load through successive layers and deforms with the subgrade; a rigid slab bridges over it in **flexure** — which is why the two are designed by completely different methods.

questions.stem: Consolidation settlement is calculated for:
options: Sand layer and when water table is far below
Sand layer with water table below the base of footing
Clay layer with water table at ground surface
questions.solution:
**Clay layer with water table at ground surface.**

Consolidation is the **time-dependent** expulsion of pore water from a saturated fine-grained soil under load. It therefore needs two things at once, both present only in option (c):

1. **Saturation** — the water table at ground level ensures the clay is fully saturated, so there is pore water to expel.
2. **Low permeability** — clay drains so slowly that excess pore pressure dissipates over months or years, which is what makes the settlement "consolidation" rather than immediate.

In **sand**, permeability is high, drainage is essentially instantaneous, and settlement occurs as the load is applied — treated as immediate/elastic settlement, not consolidation.

So consolidation settlement is a **clay** problem; sands are checked for immediate settlement and liquefaction instead.

examTip.trick: Consolidation needs three things at once: a **saturated, compressible, low-permeability** layer. Clay below the water table is exactly that; sand drains too fast and rock does not compress.
examTip.mnemonic: **Clay + water = consolidation, and it takes years.** Sand settles almost entirely **during construction**, so it is computed by elastic methods instead. Applying consolidation theory to sand is a genuine error.

questions.stem: In resource levelling, which of the following is the constraint?
questions.solution:
**Resources.**

The two techniques are mirror images of one another, and the examination tests exactly which is fixed:

| Technique | Constraint (fixed) | What is allowed to change | Aim |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Resource levelling** | **Resources** | Project duration may extend | Fit the work to the resources available |
| Resource smoothing | Time (project duration) | Resource usage within float | Even out peaks and troughs in demand |

So in **levelling** you have a hard ceiling on resources — say only four excavators exist — and activities are rescheduled, delaying the project if necessary, so that ceiling is never breached.

In **smoothing** the completion date is sacred; activities are shifted only within their available float to flatten the resource histogram.

Mnemonic: **L**evelling limits **L**abour/resources; s**m**oothing maintains the **m**ilestone date.

examTip.trap: Time and cost are the tempting answers, but they are what resource levelling **sacrifices** — the whole point is that resources are the binding constraint.
examTip.trick: Keep the two apart: **resource LEVELLING** smooths the resource profile within the available float, keeping the project duration fixed. **Resource SMOOTHING/allocation** accepts a longer duration to respect a hard resource limit.
examTip.mnemonic: **Levelling: fixed time, smoother resources. Allocation: fixed resources, longer time.**

questions.stem: For incremental increase analysis, initial investment must be:
questions.solution:
**Minimum.**

Incremental (marginal) analysis compares mutually exclusive alternatives by asking whether each *extra* rupee of investment earns its keep. The procedure fixes the starting point:

1. Rank all alternatives in **increasing order of initial investment**.
2. Take the alternative with the **smallest** initial investment as the current "defender" (the do-nothing or cheapest option).
3. Compute the incremental cash flow to the next-larger alternative, and its incremental rate of return, Δ IRR.
4. If Δ IRR ≥ MARR, the larger alternative becomes the defender; otherwise it is rejected.
5. Repeat until one alternative survives.

Starting from the **minimum** investment is essential — starting anywhere else would leave a cheaper, possibly superior option untested, and the increments would no longer be positive.

examTip.trick: Incremental analysis compares alternatives **two at a time**, always asking whether the **extra** investment earns its keep. So you must start from the **cheapest** option and work upward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rank by increasing investment, then test each increment.** If the incremental rate of return beats the minimum attractive rate, step up; otherwise stay. Starting from the largest option inverts every subsequent comparison.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the unsafe share?
questions.solution:
**Primary (ordinary/equity) shares.**

Risk follows the order of repayment when a company is wound up or is in loss. Those paid last carry the most risk:

| Instrument | Claim priority | Return | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Debentures** | **First** — a loan, secured | Fixed interest, payable even in a loss year | Lowest |
| Preference shares | Second | Fixed dividend, ahead of ordinary | Moderate |
| **Primary / ordinary (equity) shares** | **Last** | Residual dividend only if profit remains | **Highest** |

A company in loss must still service its debentures, may skip the preference dividend, and will almost certainly pay the ordinary shareholder nothing. The ordinary shareholder is also last in the queue on liquidation, so the capital itself is at risk.

Hence ordinary shares carry the greatest risk, and are compensated by the greatest potential return — the risk–return trade-off in its plainest form.

examTip.trick: Ranking by risk: **debentures and bonds** are debt and are paid first; **preference shares** get a fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders; **primary/ordinary (equity) shares** are paid last and carry the residual risk.
examTip.mnemonic: **Last in the queue, highest risk, highest potential return.** Equity holders own what is left after everyone else is paid — which in a liquidation is often nothing.

questions.stem: The minimum value of the 15-minute peak hour factor on a section of a road is:
questions.solution:
**0.25.**

The peak hour factor compares the whole peak hour with its busiest 15-minute slice:

> PHF = V_{hour} / (4 × V_{15,peak})

**The minimum is a limiting case.** Suppose every vehicle in the hour arrives inside one 15-minute period, so V_{hour} = V_{15,peak}. Then

> PHF = V / (4V) = **0.25**

That is the most extreme concentration possible, so PHF can never fall below 0.25.

**The maximum** is the opposite extreme: perfectly uniform flow, four equal quarters, V_{15} = V/4, giving PHF = V/(4 × V/4) = **1.0**.

So **0.25 ≤ PHF ≤ 1.0** always, with typical urban values of 0.85–0.95. A low PHF signals very peaked demand and governs the design hourly volume.

examTip.trick: **PHF = hourly volume / (4 × peak 15-minute volume).** If all the traffic arrived in one 15-minute burst, the hourly volume would equal that burst, giving PHF = 1/4 = **0.25**.
examTip.mnemonic: **PHF ranges 0.25 to 1.00** — 1.00 means perfectly uniform flow, 0.25 the most extreme possible peaking. Typical urban values are 0.85–0.95.

questions.stem: In a mass haul diagram, if the end is negative what does it mean?
questions.solution:
**Borrow** — extra earth must be brought in.

A mass haul diagram plots the **cumulative** volume of cut minus fill along the chainage, with cut taken positive and fill negative. The ordinate at any point is therefore the net earth available up to that point.

Reading the final ordinate:

| Final ordinate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negative** | Fill exceeds cut → **borrow** required from outside |
| Positive | Cut exceeds fill → **surplus**, to be wasted or spoiled |
| Zero | Cut and fill **balance** exactly |

Other features worth knowing: a **rising** curve means cutting, a **falling** curve means filling, a **maximum or minimum** marks a change from cut to fill, and a **balancing line** (horizontal chord) cuts the curve at points between which earthwork balances — the length of that chord is the haul distance.

examTip.trick: In a mass haul diagram the ordinate is **cumulative cut minus fill**. A **rising** curve means cut (excess material); a **falling** curve means fill. Ending below the datum means fill exceeded cut over the whole job.
examTip.mnemonic: **Negative at the end = not enough material = BORROW.** Positive at the end = surplus = **waste (spoil)**. The diagram's other use is finding the **economical haul distance** and balancing points.

questions.stem: Which is the weakest bonding in brick masonry?
questions.solution:
**Raking bond.**

In a raking bond the bricks of the internal filler courses are laid **at an angle** to the face of the wall, rather than parallel or perpendicular to it. It is not a structural face bond at all — it is used to fill the middle of a very thick wall, and to tie the wall longitudinally at intervals of four to eight courses. Because the bricks are inclined, the courses lack the continuous horizontal bedding and the regular overlap that give a wall its strength, so on its own it is the weakest arrangement of the four.

How the others compare, which is the more commonly asked half:

| Bond | Character |
|---|---|
| **English bond** | **Strongest.** Alternate courses of headers and stretchers |
| Flemish bond | Better appearance, weaker than English; header and stretcher alternate in the *same* course |
| Header bond | Headers only; used for curved walls and footings, weak along the wall |
| **Raking bond** | **Filler bond** for thick walls; least structural continuity |

So remember the pair together: **English strongest, raking weakest.**

examTip.trick: Rank the bonds by strength: **English** strongest (alternate header and stretcher courses, no continuous internal vertical joint), **Flemish** next (better appearance), **stretcher/header** for half-brick and curved work, and **raking** bonds weakest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Raking bonds (herringbone, diagonal) are decorative fill for thick walls, not structural bonds.** They are used in the interior of very thick walls to tie the outer skins, never for strength.

questions.stem: Which lime is used in lime mortar?
questions.solution:
**Hydraulic lime.**

Hydraulic lime is burnt from limestone containing **5–30% clay**. The clay contributes silica and alumina, which let the lime set by hydration — that is, **under water as well as in air**. That is exactly what a masonry mortar needs, so hydraulic lime is the lime used in lime mortar.

Why not the others:
- **Quick lime** (CaO) is the raw burnt product. It must be **slaked** with water before use; applied directly it would expand and disrupt the work.
- **Fat lime** (< 5% clay) sets only in air, by slowly absorbing CO_{2} (carbonation). It suits whitewashing and plastering, not structural mortar.
- **Poor lime** (> 30% clay, the "ump lime" of the option) slakes sluggishly and gives a weak mortar.

The standard exam pairing: **fat lime → air setting, whitewash; hydraulic lime → water setting, mortar.** Where both appear as options for mortar, choose hydraulic lime.

examTip.trick: Three limes by hydraulicity: **fat lime** (pure, sets only by carbonation, needs air), **hydraulic lime** (contains clay, **sets under water**), **poor lime** (too much impurity, weak).
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydraulic lime sets in water — the name says so.** Fat lime cannot be used for masonry mortar in damp conditions because it never sets in the wall's interior, where CO₂ cannot reach.

questions.stem: At how much minimum depth below soil is footing provided?
questions.solution:
**500 mm (0.50 m) below natural ground level.**

IS 1080 requires that all footings extend to a depth of at least **0.50 m** below natural ground level. The reasons are practical:

- Below the zone of **seasonal moisture movement**, so the soil neither swells nor shrinks under the footing.
- Below the depth disturbed by **frost action, erosion and surface activity**.
- Onto soil that has not been loosened by topsoil, roots or organic matter.

The exception the code allows: on **rock or other weather-resisting natural ground**, stripping the topsoil may be enough — the surface is then cleaned to give a sound bearing, and the 0.5 m rule does not apply.

Do not confuse this minimum depth with the **minimum thickness** of a footing, which IS 456 puts at 150 mm for a footing on soil (300 mm over piles).

examTip.trick: The 500 mm minimum is practical, not analytical — it gets the footing below topsoil, organic matter and the zone of surface disturbance.
examTip.mnemonic: **500 mm is the FLOOR, not the answer.** The real depth is whichever is deepest of: below topsoil, below seasonal moisture change, below frost, and **below SCOUR** — which usually governs near any watercourse and can dominate everything else.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a profession?
options: It enjoys a high level of public trust and confidence
There are published authoritative performance and ethical standards
All of the above are characteristics of a profession
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

A profession is distinguished from an ordinary occupation by a recognised cluster of features, and the three listed are all standard members of that list:

- **Public trust and confidence** — the work affects public safety, so society extends trust and, in return, expects accountability.
- **Organisation into associations** — a professional body (in Nepal, the Nepal Engineers' Association) and a statutory regulator (the Nepal Engineering Council).
- **Published performance and ethical standards** — a written code of ethics and technical standards against which conduct can be judged.

The usual full list also includes: a substantial body of specialised knowledge acquired by prolonged formal education; **licensure or registration** to practise; exercise of independent professional judgement; a duty to place public welfare above personal or client interest; and self-regulation with disciplinary powers.

When an "all of the above" option gathers several genuine attributes of a definition, it is almost always the intended answer.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" questions reward reading every option. Here each listed attribute genuinely belongs to a profession.
examTip.trick: The recognised marks of a profession: **specialised knowledge from long training, a code of ethics, self-regulation through a body, service to the public interest, and licensure**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Knowledge, ethics, self-regulation, public service.** Registration with the NEC is precisely the licensure element for engineering in Nepal.

questions.stem: In case of a propped cantilever beam under UDL, the plastic hinge is located at what distance from the propped end?
questions.solution:
**0.414L from the propped end.**

A propped cantilever carrying a UDL is indeterminate to the first degree, so collapse needs **two** hinges: one forms at the **fixed end**, and a second must form in the span before the mechanism is complete.

The sagging hinge forms where the free-span bending moment is a maximum, and working through the collapse mechanism puts it at

> x = (√2 − 1)L = 0.4142L  from the propped (simple) end

with the collapse load given by w_{c} = 11.66M_{p}/L².

Related distances for the same beam under UDL, which the options are drawn from:

| Quantity | Distance from propped end |
|---|---|
| **Plastic hinge** | **0.414L** |
| Maximum sagging moment (elastic) | 0.375L = 3L/8 |
| Point of contraflexure (elastic) | 0.75L = 3L/4 |

So 0.414L is the plastic answer; 3L/8 and 3L/4 belong to the elastic analysis of the same beam.

examTip.trick: In plastic analysis the propped cantilever forms **two** hinges — one at the fixed end and one in the span. The span hinge is at **0.414L** from the propped end, where 0.414 = √2 − 1.
examTip.mnemonic: **√2 − 1 = 0.414.** Note this is the **PLASTIC** hinge position, not the elastic maximum-moment position (0.375L). Confusing the two is the trap — plastic analysis relocates the peak because the fixed end has already yielded.

questions.stem: Why is a circular column generally not used?
questions.solution:
**Difficult to connect to beam.**

The objection is constructional, not structural. A rectangular column offers **flat faces** into which a beam frames squarely: the beam soffit and sides meet a plane surface, reinforcement anchors cleanly, and formwork is simple carpentry. Against a curved face, the beam–column joint needs awkward detailing, the shuttering must be curved, and bar bending and cover control both become fiddly.

Why the other options are wrong on their own terms:
- **Uneconomical** — not inherently; a circular column can be economical, and it uses helical (spiral) reinforcement efficiently.
- **Low load carrying capacity** — the opposite is true. IS 456 permits a **1.05 multiplier** on the strength of a column with helical reinforcement, precisely because the spiral confines the core. A circular column is also equally stiff about every axis, which is why it is preferred for bridge piers and piles, where framing is not an issue.

So circular columns are used freely where nothing has to frame into them, and avoided in beam–column building frames.

examTip.trick: The objection is **buildability**, not capacity — a circular column is actually efficient structurally and is excellent for spirally reinforced compression members.
examTip.mnemonic: **A beam frames squarely into a flat face, awkwardly into a curve.** Which is why circular columns appear where beams do not frame in — piers, piles, and free-standing columns — and rectangular ones appear in framed buildings.

questions.stem: The Bernoulli equation states that:
options: Discharge is constant throughout the section
Energy is constant for one streamline and is different from another streamline
Energy is constant throughout the flow
questions.solution:
**Energy is constant along one streamline, and may differ from streamline to streamline.**

Bernoulli's equation,

> p/γ + v²/2g + z = constant

is obtained by integrating Euler's equation **along a streamline**. The constant of integration therefore belongs to *that* streamline. Two different streamlines in the same flow can perfectly well carry different total heads — for example in a boundary layer, or in flow with vorticity.

The constant becomes the same for **all** streamlines only in the special case of **irrotational** flow, which is an extra assumption, not part of the statement.

Why the others are wrong:
- **(a)** is the continuity equation (Q = A₁v₁ = A₂v₂), a statement of mass conservation, not energy.
- **(c)** overclaims — it holds only for irrotational flow.

Also recall the assumptions: steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow, along a streamline. Real flows need a loss term: p₁/γ + v₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/γ + v₂²/2g + z₂ + h_{L}.

examTip.trick: Bernoulli's constant applies **along a streamline**. Only if the flow is also **irrotational** does the same constant hold across the whole field.
examTip.mnemonic: **One streamline, one constant.** That is exactly why a **free vortex** (irrotational, no torque) permits Bernoulli between radii, while a **forced vortex** (driven by torque, energy added) does not.

questions.stem: Slump test is used to measure:
questions.solution:
**Consistency** (and hence workability).

The slump test measures how far a cone of fresh concrete subsides under its own weight once the mould is lifted — a direct index of consistency, and the simplest field measure of **workability**.

Apparatus and limits worth knowing (IS 1199): a frustum of a cone, **bottom 200 mm, top 100 mm, height 300 mm**, filled in three layers, each tamped 25 times with a 16 mm rod.

Typical slump values:

| Construction | Slump (mm) |
|---|---|
| Road pavement, mass concrete | 20 – 50 |
| Beams, slabs, columns (normal RCC) | 50 – 100 |
| Heavily reinforced / congested sections | 100 – 150 |
| Pumped concrete | 100 – 150 |

Match the other options to their own tests: **setting time → Vicat apparatus**; **soundness → Le Chatelier apparatus or autoclave**; **water content of aggregate → oven drying**. Note also that slump is unsuitable for very dry mixes, where the **compaction factor** or **Vee-Bee** test is used instead.

examTip.trap: "Strength" is the standard wrong answer. A high slump from excess water means **weaker** concrete, not stronger.
examTip.trick: Slump measures the **yield stress** of the fresh mix — how easily it will flow and compact. It says nothing about hardened properties.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump is about PLACING, not about strength.** For very dry mixes slump reads near zero and is useless; use the **compaction factor** or **vee-bee** test instead.

questions.stem: Moisture condition of aggregate used in concrete is:
questions.solution:
**Saturated surface dry (SSD).**

SSD is the reference condition for mix design: the aggregate pores are **full of water** but there is **no free water on the surface**. In that state the aggregate neither absorbs water from the mix nor contributes water to it, so the water–cement ratio actually achieved is the one that was designed.

The four moisture states, in order of increasing water:

| State | Pores | Surface | Effect on the mix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oven dry** | Empty | Dry | Absorbs mix water; stiffens the concrete, raises effective w/c error |
| Air dry | Partly filled | Dry | Absorbs some mix water |
| **Saturated surface dry** | **Full** | **Dry** | **Neutral — the design reference** |
| Wet (damp) | Full | Free water | Adds water; raises w/c and lowers strength |

On site aggregate is almost never at SSD, so the batch water is **corrected** for free surface moisture or for absorption. Failing to make that correction is a common cause of a mix under-performing its design strength.

examTip.trick: **SSD** means the aggregate's pores are full but its surface is dry — so it neither **absorbs** mix water nor **adds** free water to the mix. It is the neutral reference condition.
examTip.mnemonic: **SSD is the zero point.** Drier than SSD and the aggregate steals mix water (the concrete stiffens); wetter and it contributes water (the w/c ratio rises and strength falls). On site, aggregate moisture must be measured and the batch water corrected — every time.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an impulse turbine?
questions.solution:
**Pelton.**

In an **impulse** turbine the whole of the available head is converted to **kinetic energy in a nozzle before** the water strikes the runner, so at inlet the energy is purely kinetic and the runner turns at atmospheric pressure. The Pelton wheel is the classic example.

In a **reaction** turbine the runner is fully submerged and there is a pressure drop **across** the runner itself, so the water arrives with both pressure and kinetic energy.

| | Impulse | Reaction |
|---|---|---|
| Example | **Pelton**, Turgo, cross-flow | **Francis, Kaplan, propeller** |
| Energy at inlet | Kinetic only | Kinetic + pressure |
| Head | High (> 250 m) | Medium (Francis) to low (Kaplan) |
| Discharge | Low | High |
| Specific speed | Low (10–35) | Medium to high |
| Casing | Not pressurised | Pressurised (scroll case) |
| **Draft tube** | **Not required** | **Required** |

The last row is examined constantly, and appears again as Q57 of this very paper: a Pelton wheel needs no draft tube because it discharges freely to the tailrace.

examTip.trick: Split by mechanism: an **impulse** turbine converts all the head to velocity in a nozzle and the runner works at atmospheric pressure. A **reaction** turbine has pressure changing across the runner, which therefore runs full.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pelton is the only common impulse turbine; Francis and Kaplan are reaction.** Match to head: **Pelton high head/low flow** (Nepal's Himalayan streams), **Francis medium**, **Kaplan low head/high flow**. A Pelton bucket runs at **u = V/2** for maximum power.

questions.stem: The mixture of cement, sand and coarse aggregate is increased by what percentage to get the dry volume of concrete?
questions.solution:
**50–55%** — conventionally taken as **54%**.

Dry, loose materials contain air voids that disappear once the mix is compacted with water. To obtain a given **wet** volume of finished concrete you must therefore batch a larger **dry** volume:

> Dry volume = Wet volume × 1.54

Where the 54% comes from:
- Dry coarse aggregate carries roughly **33–34%** voids.
- Dry sand carries roughly **20%** voids.
- Cement is so fine that its contribution is negligible.
- Together these come to about **54%**.

**Worked example — 1 m³ of M20 (1 : 1.5 : 3), total parts = 5.5:**
> Dry volume = 1 × 1.54 = 1.54 m³
> Cement = 1.54 × 1/5.5 = 0.28 m³ ≈ 8 bags (403 kg)
> Sand = 1.54 × 1.5/5.5 = 0.42 m³
> Coarse aggregate = 1.54 × 3/5.5 = 0.84 m³

Some texts use 1.52 or 1.57; any figure in the **50–55%** band is the intended answer.

examTip.trick: Dry ingredients have voids between the particles; adding water and compacting fills them, so the **wet volume is LESS than the sum of the dry volumes**. The dry quantity must therefore be increased by roughly half again.
examTip.mnemonic: **Multiply the wet volume by about 1.54 to get the dry volume.** This is why a nominal 1:2:4 mix by volume needs 1.54 m³ of dry material per cubic metre of finished concrete.

questions.stem: In a slab, the minimum thickness is designed to resist:
questions.solution:
**Compression** — the option standing in for flexure.

A slab is a flexural member. Its thickness has to provide a large enough **lever arm** and enough depth of concrete in the **compression zone** to develop the bending moment, since concrete carries the compression while the steel carries the tension. Of the four options only compression names a flexural action, so it is the intended answer.

**Worth being precise about, because the question is loosely framed:** in real design the thickness of a slab is almost never governed by strength at all. It is governed by **deflection control**, applied through the span-to-effective-depth limits of IS 456 cl. 23.2.1:

| Support condition | Basic span/depth |
|---|---|
| Cantilever | 7 |
| Simply supported | 20 |
| Continuous | 26 |

modified by the tension-steel percentage. Shear rarely governs a slab, and **punching (two-way) shear** governs only locally around a column in a flat slab.

So: choose compression here, but carry the real rule — **slab depth is fixed by deflection, then checked for flexure and shear.**

examTip.trick: For a slab the depth is not usually set by bending strength at all — a thin slab has ample moment capacity. What governs is **stiffness (deflection)** and the compressive block depth at the top face.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slabs are governed by DEFLECTION, not by moment** — hence the span/depth rules (IS 456: 20 simply supported, 26 continuous, 7 cantilever). Slabs also rarely need shear reinforcement, which is why keeping them thick enough matters.

questions.stem: In which scale are maps drawn?
questions.solution:
**Reducing scale.**

A map represents a piece of the earth's surface on a sheet of paper, so the ground must always be shrunk. The representative fraction is therefore always less than one — 1:1000, 1:50 000 and so on — which is by definition a **reducing** scale.

An **enlarging** scale (RF greater than 1) is used for *drawings* of very small objects, such as a watch component or a bolt thread, where the drawing is bigger than the thing itself. A **full-size** scale (1:1) is used for ordinary machine drawings. Neither applies to a map.

Useful map classification by scale:

| Map | Representative fraction |
|---|---|
| Cadastral / plan | 1:500 to 1:5 000 |
| Topographic | 1:25 000 to 1:250 000 |
| Geographical / atlas | smaller than 1:1 000 000 |

A **large-scale** map covers a small area in great detail (1:500); a **small-scale** map covers a large area with little detail (1:1 000 000) — a wording trap in its own right.

examTip.trick: Every map is drawn **smaller** than reality, so the representative fraction is less than one — a **reducing** scale.
examTip.mnemonic: **Large scale means a SMALL area shown in great detail** (1:1000); **small scale means a LARGE area in little detail** (1:1 000 000). The naming feels backwards until you remember it refers to the size of the **fraction**, not the area.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pile foundation?
questions.solution:
**Deep foundation.**

The dividing line is the ratio of depth to width: a foundation is **shallow** when its depth of embedment D is less than about its width B (D/B ≤ 1), and **deep** when D is much greater than B. A pile is long and slender, so it is emphatically deep — and it works by carrying load **past** weak surface strata to a competent stratum below, through end bearing and skin friction.

| Shallow foundations | Deep foundations |
|---|---|
| Isolated (spread) footing | **Pile** |
| Combined footing | Pier / drilled shaft |
| Strip / wall footing | Caisson / well foundation |
| Raft (mat) | Pile-raft |

An **open foundation** is another name for a shallow footing built in an open excavation, so option (d) is the opposite of a pile.

When piles are chosen: weak or compressible topsoil, heavy or concentrated loads, uplift or lateral load (as under a transmission tower), scour risk at a bridge pier, or expansive soil where the founding level must sit below the active zone.

examTip.trick: The classification is by **load transfer**, not merely depth: a shallow foundation delivers load through its **base**; a deep one adds **shaft friction** over many diameters.
examTip.mnemonic: **D_f/B ≤ 1 shallow, > 1 deep.** Piles, piers and wells are deep; pads, strips, combined footings and **rafts** are all shallow — a raft is shallow however large it is.

questions.stem: A Newtonian fluid is one which:
options: Does not follow Newton's law of viscosity
Follows that shear stress is directly proportional to velocity gradient
questions.solution:
**Shear stress is directly proportional to the velocity gradient.**

Newton's law of viscosity:

> τ = μ (du/dy)

A fluid is **Newtonian** when this holds with **μ constant** — so a plot of shear stress against rate of shear strain is a **straight line through the origin**, whose slope is the dynamic viscosity. Water, air, kerosene, thin oils and glycerine all behave this way.

Non-Newtonian behaviour, for contrast:

| Type | Behaviour | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dilatant (shear-thickening) | μ rises with shear rate | Sugar solution, quicksand slurry |
| Pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) | μ falls with shear rate | Paint, blood, polymer melt |
| Bingham plastic | Needs a yield stress before flowing | Toothpaste, drilling mud, fresh concrete |
| Ideal / inviscid | μ = 0, no shear stress | A theoretical fluid only |

Option (d) is a distractor worth noting: every **real** fluid has viscosity, but not every real fluid is Newtonian — paint and toothpaste are real and non-Newtonian.

examTip.trick: **τ = μ(du/dy)** — a **straight line through the origin**. Both conditions matter: linearity, and passing through the origin (no yield stress).
examTip.mnemonic: **Water, air and most oils are Newtonian. Fresh CONCRETE, drilling mud and toothpaste are BINGHAM PLASTICS** — they need a yield stress before they move at all, which is why concrete holds its slump shape and why vibration is needed to make it flow.

questions.stem: Length of hydraulic jump is equal to:
options: Greater than 10 times the jump height
questions.solution:
**5 to 7 times the height of the jump.**

The length of a hydraulic jump is the distance from the section just upstream of the jump to the section where the surface levels out downstream. It cannot be derived from momentum theory — momentum gives the **depths**, not the length — so it comes from experiment. For a rectangular channel the accepted result is

> L_{j} ≈ 5 to 7 times the height of the jump, (y₂ − y₁)

and it is usually quoted as **5 to 7 times y₂** as well, since y₂ dominates.

What momentum theory *does* give, and is asked alongside:

> y₂/y₁ = ½ (√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)

Energy loss in the jump:

> E_{L} = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4y₁y₂)

Classification by upstream Froude number: undular (1–1.7), weak (1.7–2.5), oscillating (2.5–4.5), **steady (4.5–9, the type used in stilling basins)**, strong (> 9).

The length matters because it fixes the length of the **stilling basin** downstream of a spillway or weir.

examTip.trick: No theory predicts the jump length — it is entirely **empirical**, and the usual working value is **5 to 7 times the sequent depth y₂** (commonly taken as 6y₂).
examTip.mnemonic: **Basin length ≈ 6 y₂.** Baffle blocks and an end sill shorten it by 30–50%, which is why they earn their cost. The critical design risk remains the **tailwater**: too little and the jump sweeps out of the paved basin and undermines it.

questions.stem: Which method gives an accurate estimate of average rainfall in a hilly area catchment?
questions.solution:
**Isohyetal method.**

An isohyet is a contour of equal rainfall. The method draws these contours from the gauge records and computes

> P̄ = Σ [ A_{i} × (P_{i} + P_{i+1})/2 ] / ΣA

where A_{i} is the area between two adjacent isohyets.

It is the most accurate method in **hilly terrain** because the person drawing the isohyets can incorporate knowledge that the gauge data alone does not contain — orographic effect, the rain shadow on the lee slope, aspect, and the systematic increase of rainfall with elevation. It is not a purely mechanical weighting, and that is exactly its strength in mountains.

The alternatives:

| Method | Basis | Best suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **Isohyetal** | Area between rainfall contours | **Hilly / orographic catchments** |
| Thiessen polygon | Area of polygon nearest each gauge | Reasonably flat area, non-uniform gauge spacing |
| Arithmetic mean | Simple average | Flat area, uniformly spaced gauges, little variation |
| Normal ratio | — | **Estimating a missing record**, not areal average |

Note that option (b) answers a different question altogether: the normal ratio method fills in **missing** rainfall data at a station.

examTip.trick: The isohyetal method is the only one where the person drawing the lines can build in **knowledge of the terrain** — pulling contours to follow ridges and valleys where orographic effects are known.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic mean → Thiessen (gauge spacing) → Isohyetal (spacing AND terrain).** In Nepal the orographic gradient is enormous — Pokhara ~4000 mm against Jomsom ~250 mm — so a purely geometric method is weak in the hills.

questions.stem: Which among the following methods is very accurate for rain gauging?
questions.solution:
**Recording type (autographic) rain gauge.**

Read the question carefully — it asks about **rain gauging**, that is the act of *measuring* rainfall, not about averaging records over an area. The other three options are all areal-averaging techniques and belong to the previous question.

A **recording** gauge produces a continuous trace of accumulated rainfall against time, so it yields not only the total depth but also the **intensity, duration and temporal pattern** of a storm — none of which a non-recording gauge can give. That information is indispensable for deriving intensity–duration–frequency curves, unit hydrographs and drainage design.

The three recording types:

| Type | Principle |
|---|---|
| **Tipping bucket** | A small bucket tips at each fixed increment, closing a circuit |
| **Weighing bucket** | Weight of accumulated rain recorded continuously |
| **Float (natural syphon)** | Float rises with collected water; syphons out automatically |

Against these, the **Symon's non-recording gauge** gives only a single total read manually, usually once every 24 hours.

So the contrast to hold: **Q35 was about averaging over an area (isohyetal); Q36 is about the instrument (recording gauge).**

examTip.trick: A non-recording gauge gives only a **daily total**. A recording gauge gives the **intensity trace**, which is what storm drainage and flood design actually require — a daily total cannot distinguish a cloudburst from steady rain.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only a recording gauge gives INTENSITY.** The tipping-bucket type is the practical standard: each 0.25 mm tips a bucket and closes a switch, so the record is digital and easily telemetered.

questions.stem: In case of long columns, direct stress is …… compared to bending stress.
questions.solution:
**Negligible.**

A long (slender) column fails by **buckling**, not by crushing. As soon as it deflects laterally by an amount e, the axial load P acts at an eccentricity and generates a bending moment P·e. Because the slenderness ratio is large, that lateral deflection — and hence the bending moment — grows very rapidly, and the bending stress swamps the direct stress P/A.

So for design purposes the direct stress in a long column is treated as negligible, and the member is governed by Euler's buckling load:

> P_{cr} = π²EI / l_{e}²  , equivalently  σ_{cr} = π²E / (l_{e}/k)²

The contrast with the other extreme:

| | Short column | Long column |
|---|---|---|
| Slenderness ratio | Low (< ~32 for steel; < 12 for RCC) | High |
| Mode of failure | **Crushing** | **Buckling** |
| Governing stress | **Direct** (P/A) | **Bending** |
| Design basis | Compressive strength | Euler / Rankine, stiffness EI |

A **medium** column fails by a combination of both and is handled by the Rankine–Gordon formula.

Note too that buckling depends on **stiffness (E and I)**, not on strength — so a higher-grade steel does not raise the buckling load of a slender strut at all.

examTip.trick: In a long (slender) column, buckling means the member deflects laterally, so the **bending stress from the eccentric deflection dominates** and the direct axial stress P/A becomes a small part of the total.
examTip.mnemonic: **Short columns crush (direct stress governs); long columns buckle (bending governs).** The dividing quantity is the **slenderness ratio L_e/r** — and Euler's formula contains no strength term at all, only E and geometry.

questions.stem: In case of cavity walls where both walls are load bearing, the effective thickness is:
options: 2/3 of sum of thickness of both walls
questions.solution:
**Larger of (b) and (c)** — the greater of the thicker leaf and two-thirds of the sum.

IS 1905 cl. 4.5.3 states that for a cavity wall in which **both leaves are loaded**, the effective thickness is

> t_{eff} = greater of  { ⅔ (t₁ + t₂) ,  t_{thicker leaf} }

Both candidates must be evaluated and the larger taken — which is exactly what option (d) says.

**Worked check, two leaves of 100 mm and 200 mm:**
> ⅔ (100 + 200) = 200 mm
> thicker leaf = 200 mm
> t_{eff} = **200 mm** — here the two happen to coincide.

**Two leaves of 100 mm and 100 mm:**
> ⅔ (100 + 100) = 133 mm
> thicker leaf = 100 mm
> t_{eff} = **133 mm** — here the two-thirds rule governs, and taking only the thicker leaf would under-estimate the wall by a third.

That second case is precisely why the code requires the greater of the two, and why answering "thickness of the stronger wall" alone is unsafe. Effective thickness then feeds the slenderness ratio, SR = effective height / effective thickness, which is capped at 27 for load-bearing masonry.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The widely-copied answer sheet gives (b), "thickness of the stronger wall". That is wrong: it ignores the two-thirds criterion, which governs whenever the two leaves are of similar thickness, and would over-estimate the slenderness capacity of the wall. IS 1905 requires the greater of the two values, so the answer is (d).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (b), the thickness of the stronger wall. IS 1905 cl. 4.5.3 requires the GREATER of two-thirds the sum of the two leaf thicknesses and the thickness of the thicker leaf. For two equal 100 mm leaves the two-thirds rule gives 133 mm against 100 mm, so the key would under-estimate effective thickness by a third. Answer corrected to (d).

examTip.trick: When both leaves carry load, the effective thickness cannot be taken as the sum of the two leaves plus the void. Codes take the **greater** of two-thirds the sum of the actual thicknesses, or the thickness of the **thicker** leaf alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Take the larger of the two permitted values.** The cavity contributes nothing structurally — it is there for **damp exclusion and insulation**, and it must be kept clear of mortar droppings or it bridges and defeats both purposes.

questions.stem: Harmful bacteria are called:
questions.solution:
**Pathogens.**

A pathogen is any organism capable of causing disease. The term is defined by **effect on the host**, which is what the question asks about.

The distractors are classified on entirely different bases:
- **Aerobic / anaerobic** classify bacteria by whether they need **free oxygen**. This says nothing about harm — the aerobic bacteria in an activated sludge plant are the useful workhorses of sewage treatment, while some anaerobes are harmless and others deadly.
- **Parasite** describes a *mode of life* — living on or in a host at the host's expense. Parasites are usually protozoa or helminths rather than bacteria.

Water-borne pathogens and their diseases, a standard exam list:

| Organism | Disease |
|---|---|
| *Vibrio cholerae* | Cholera |
| *Salmonella typhi* | Typhoid |
| *Shigella* | Bacillary dysentery |
| *Entamoeba histolytica* | Amoebic dysentery |
| Hepatitis A virus | Infectious hepatitis |

Because testing for each pathogen is impractical, water quality is judged by an **indicator organism** — *E. coli* / total coliforms. Their presence signals faecal contamination and hence the possible presence of pathogens; drinking water standards require **zero E. coli per 100 mL**.

examTip.trick: **Pathogen** means, literally, disease-producer. Not all bacteria are pathogens — most are harmless or beneficial, which is why the word exists.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water quality is monitored by INDICATOR organisms (E. coli, faecal coliform), not by testing for every pathogen** — indicators are easy to count and their presence signals faecal contamination. The standard for drinking water is **zero E. coli per 100 ml**.

questions.stem: What is the opening spacing of bars in case of a coarse screen?
questions.solution:
**50 mm.**

Screening is the **first** unit operation in both water and wastewater treatment, and its job is to intercept large floating and suspended matter — rags, plastics, sticks, leaves — that would otherwise damage pumps or clog the plant downstream.

Screens are graded by the clear opening between bars:

| Screen | Clear opening | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse (bar rack)** | **≈ 50 mm and above** | Protects pumps from large debris |
| Medium | 20 – 50 mm | Intercepts smaller floating matter |
| Fine | < 20 mm (often 6 – 15 mm) | Removes finer solids; used sparingly, clogs readily |

Design points that accompany this:
- Bars are set at **30° to 60°** to the horizontal so the rake can clear them.
- Approach velocity is kept at about **0.6 to 1.0 m/s** — fast enough that grit does not settle in the channel, slow enough that solids are not forced through the bars.
- Head loss through a clean bar screen is small but rises sharply as it blinds, so cleaning is either manual (small plants) or mechanical (large plants).

Screening precedes **grit removal**, which takes out sand and inorganic particles, and then primary sedimentation.

examTip.trick: Screens are graded by opening: **coarse (bar) screens 50–75 mm**, **medium 20–50 mm**, **fine 6–20 mm**, and micro-screens below that.
examTip.mnemonic: **Coarse screen first, to protect the pumps** — it removes rags, sticks and debris that would wreck the machinery downstream. It is deliberately the first unit in the treatment train.

questions.stem: An inverted siphon is provided when:
questions.solution:
**A sewer crosses a river** (or any depression, cut or obstruction).

An inverted siphon — also called a depressed sewer — is a length of sewer dropped **below** the hydraulic gradient line to pass under a river, a railway cutting or a subway, and then brought back up on the far side.

The name is a misnomer: there is no siphon action and no vacuum. In fact the pipe must be kept **completely full and under positive pressure** throughout, unlike the open-channel gravity flow of an ordinary sewer.

Design requirements, all examined:
- **Self-cleansing velocity of at least 0.9 to 1.2 m/s** must be maintained, since anything that settles here cannot be flushed out easily.
- Because sewage flow varies widely through the day, **two or three parallel barrels** of differing diameter are provided, brought into service progressively as flow rises, so velocity stays high even at minimum flow.
- Inlet and outlet **chambers with penstocks** allow each barrel to be isolated and rodded.

Why the others are wrong: where two sewers meet, a **junction chamber** is used; where a large drop in invert is needed, a **drop manhole**.

examTip.trick: An inverted siphon (a **depressed sewer**) dips below an obstruction and runs **full and under pressure**, unlike the rest of a gravity sewer.
examTip.mnemonic: **It runs FULL, so it cannot be self-cleansing by gravity alone** — the velocity must be kept high (at least 0.9 m/s) and it is usually built as **multiple parallel barrels** brought into service progressively, so that even low flows keep one barrel scouring.

questions.stem: Water in a canal is based on:
questions.solution:
**Gross irrigation requirement (GIR).**

The canal has to deliver not only the water the crop consumes but also everything lost on the way. Building the quantity up in stages:

| Quantity | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Consumptive use (ET) | Evaporation + transpiration by the crop |
| **Crop water requirement** | ET + special needs (leaching, land preparation) |
| **Net irrigation requirement (NIR)** | Crop requirement **minus effective rainfall** and soil moisture contribution |
| **Gross irrigation requirement (GIR)** | **NIR ÷ overall irrigation efficiency** — includes conveyance and field application losses |

> GIR = NIR / η_{overall}

Since conveyance losses in the canal (seepage and evaporation) and field application losses are real water that must physically pass the canal head, the canal is designed for **GIR**. Design for NIR and the tail-end farmers get nothing.

**Transpiration** alone (option d) is only one component of consumptive use, so it is far too small.

examTip.trick: Work outward from the crop: **net irrigation requirement** is what the crop needs; **gross** adds the **conveyance and application losses**, which are what the canal must actually carry.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design the canal for GROSS, not net.** With typical field and conveyance efficiencies the gross requirement can be **1.5 to 2 times** the net — sizing on the net figure guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.

questions.stem: What is a load factor?
options: The ratio of average load to maximum demand
The ratio of maximum demand to average load
The product of maximum demand and average load
questions.solution:
**The ratio of average load to maximum demand.**

> Load factor = average load / peak (maximum) demand
> = energy actually generated in a period / (peak demand × hours in that period)

It is always **less than or equal to 1**, and it measures how *evenly* the plant is used. A high load factor means the plant runs near its peak most of the time, so the capital cost is spread over more units of energy and the cost per unit falls.

The related factors, constantly confused with one another:

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Load factor** | **Average load / peak demand** |
| Capacity factor | Average load / installed capacity |
| Utilisation factor | Peak demand / installed capacity |
| Demand factor | Peak demand / total connected load |
| Diversity factor | Σ individual peaks / peak of the system |

Note that load factor and capacity factor coincide only when the peak demand equals the installed capacity.

**A note on the printed options.** In the original paper options (c) and (d) were printed with identical wording — "the product of max demand and average load" — which is a typographical slip in the source. Option (d) has been replaced here with a neutral "none of the above" so that the question has four distinct choices. The keyed answer (a) is unaffected.

verification.notes: The source paper printed options (c) and (d) with identical text, so the question as printed had only three distinct choices. Option (d) has been replaced with 'None of the above'. The correct answer, (a), is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **Load factor = average load / maximum demand**, and it is always **≤ 1**. A high load factor means the plant is used evenly and its capital is well utilised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load factor: how evenly. Capacity factor: how fully** (average load ÷ installed capacity). **Diversity factor** is the sum of individual maximum demands ÷ the system maximum, and it is **> 1** — because not every consumer peaks at the same moment.

questions.stem: Which energy dissipater is provided if the jump height is more than the tail water depth?
questions.solution:
**Ski jump (deflector or flip bucket).**

The choice of energy dissipater turns entirely on how the available **tail water depth** compares with the depth needed to form a hydraulic jump (the post-jump depth y₂):

| Tail water condition | Dissipater |
|---|---|
| Tail water **much less** than required y₂ | **Ski jump / deflector / flip bucket / trajectory bucket** |
| Tail water **much more** than required y₂ | **Roller bucket** (solid or slotted) |
| Tail water ≈ required y₂ | **Stilling basin** with a horizontal apron |
| Tail water varying with discharge | Sloping apron |

The question says the jump height exceeds the tail water depth — that is, there is **not enough** water downstream to drown the jump. A hydraulic jump therefore cannot form on the apron, and holding it there would drive a high-velocity jet along the river bed and scour it out.

The ski jump instead **throws the jet clear of the structure** as a free trajectory, so most of the energy is dissipated in the air and in the plunge pool well downstream, away from the dam toe. It suits high dams on sound rock, where a deep plunge pool can be tolerated — Tehri and Bhakra are classic examples.

examTip.trick: Choose the dissipater by comparing the required **sequent depth y₂** with the **available tailwater**. If the tailwater is too shallow to hold a jump, a jump-type basin cannot work.
examTip.mnemonic: **Insufficient tailwater → throw the water clear instead. That is the SKI JUMP (flip) bucket** — it hurls the jet downstream to dissipate in the air and in a plunge pool well away from the structure. Common on high dams in narrow gorges.

questions.stem: Which is used to protect the turbine and runner from damage?
questions.solution:
**Surge tank.**

When the turbine gates are closed or opened suddenly, the water in the pressure conduit cannot change velocity instantly and a pressure wave — **water hammer** — races back up the tunnel. Unchecked, the pressure rise can burst the penstock or wreck the runner and spiral casing.

A surge tank is an open-topped shaft or chamber placed at the junction of the low-pressure tunnel and the high-pressure penstock. It does two jobs:

1. **On sudden closure** it accepts the rejected water, converting the pressure surge into a harmless rise of level, so the water-hammer pressure is confined to the short penstock below it rather than the whole tunnel.
2. **On sudden opening** it supplies water immediately from storage while the flow in the long tunnel accelerates, preventing a negative pressure and cavitation.

Types: simple, restricted orifice, differential (Johnson), and inclined.

Why the others are wrong: a **penstock** is the conduit being protected, not the protection; a **powerhouse** merely houses the machinery; a **fuel tank** has no place in a hydropower plant at all. For very long conduits where a surge tank is impractical, a **pressure relief valve** serves instead.

examTip.trick: The surge tank gives the decelerating water column a **free surface** to rise into, converting a destructive pressure wave into a slow rise and fall of level.
examTip.mnemonic: **It protects only what is UPSTREAM of it** — the long low-pressure tunnel. The short penstock below still takes the full water hammer and is built for it. Place it as close to the machine as topography allows.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not related to the cross section of a road?
questions.solution:
**Gradient.**

Gradient is the rate of rise or fall of the road **along its length**. It belongs to the **vertical alignment** — the longitudinal profile — and not to the cross section at all. A cross section is a cut taken *transverse* to the centre line, so anything measured along the direction of travel cannot appear in it.

The other three are all transverse quantities and so are genuine cross-sectional elements:

| Element | Why it is cross-sectional |
|---|---|
| **Camber** | Transverse slope from crown to edge, for surface drainage (1.7–2.5% for bituminous) |
| **Super elevation** | Transverse slope on a curve, to counter centrifugal force (max 7% in plains, 10% in hills) |
| **Lanes** | Number of lanes fixes the **carriageway width** — 3.75 m single lane, 7.0 m two lane |

The full list of cross-section elements also includes shoulders, kerbs, footpaths, side drains, medians, side slopes, formation width and right of way.

The syllabus itself makes the split, listing "elements of highway cross-section" and "average and ruling gradients" as separate items.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The widely-copied answer sheet gives (c), "lanes", on the reasoning that lanes are "not directly related" to the cross section. That is wrong: the number of lanes is what determines carriageway width, one of the primary cross-sectional dimensions, and every standard cross-section drawing shows it. Gradient is the only option that is a longitudinal quantity, so the answer is (d).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (c), lanes. Lanes determine carriageway width and are a core cross-sectional element, appearing on every standard cross-section drawing. Gradient is the longitudinal slope and belongs to the vertical alignment, not the cross section, so (d) is the only correct answer.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Camber, carriageway width, shoulders and side slopes are all cross-sectional; **gradient** belongs to the longitudinal profile.
examTip.trick: Cross section = what you see looking **along** the road (a slice). Longitudinal profile = what you see from the **side** (gradients, vertical curves, summits and sags).
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross section is a slice; gradient is a slope along the length.**

questions.stem: In which stage of survey is soil survey done?
questions.solution:
**Preliminary survey.**

Highway location proceeds through four stages, each finer than the last, and **soil survey belongs to the third — the preliminary survey**, where quantitative data is collected for the alternative alignments that survived reconnaissance.

| Stage | What is done |
|---|---|
| 1. **Map study** | Desk work on topographic sheets; possible routes marked, no field visit |
| 2. **Reconnaissance** | Rapid field inspection of those routes; rough levels, obvious obstacles noted; no instruments of precision |
| 3. **Preliminary survey** | Detailed survey of alternatives: **topographic, soil and materials survey**, drainage, traffic; alternatives compared and one selected |
| 4. **Final location and detailed survey** | Selected alignment pegged on the ground; data for design and estimation |

At the preliminary stage the soil survey establishes the **subgrade** character — classification, CBR, moisture and drainage conditions, depth of water table, and the location of borrow areas and quarries. That information is essential both for pavement thickness design and for comparing the economics of the alternatives, which is the whole purpose of the stage.

A reconnaissance survey is far too coarse for this: it records only what can be seen and paced.

examTip.trick: The survey sequence runs **reconnaissance → preliminary → final location**. Detailed data collection, including soils and materials, belongs to the **preliminary** stage, once the corridor is chosen but before the centre line is fixed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reconnaissance picks the corridor; preliminary investigates it; final location pegs the centre line.** Soil survey has to come before the alignment is fixed, or the alignment cannot respond to what the soil says.

questions.stem: In case of the most economical trapezoidal section, the top width is equal to:
questions.solution:
**Double the sloping side.**

A section is most economical (most efficient) when, for a given area, the wetted perimeter is a minimum — so the discharge is a maximum. Working that condition through for a trapezoid gives two results:

1. **Half the top width equals the sloping side**, that is
> Top width = 2 × sloping side

2. **The hydraulic radius equals half the depth of flow**, R = y/2 — equivalently, a semicircle centred on the water surface and of radius y is tangent to both sides and the bed.

For the best trapezoid of all, the side slope is at **60° to the horizontal** (a half-hexagon).

The companion results for other shapes, which the options borrow from:

| Section | Most economical condition |
|---|---|
| Rectangle | b = 2y, and **R = y/2** |
| **Trapezoid** | **Top width = 2 × sloping side, R = y/2** |
| Triangle | Side slope at 45°, R = y/(2√2) |
| Circle (max velocity) | y = 0.81D, R = 0.3D |
| Circle (max discharge) | y = 0.95D |

Note that **R = y/2** is common to the rectangle and the trapezoid, which is worth remembering as a single fact.

examTip.trick: The most economical trapezoid is **half a regular hexagon** — 60° sides, top width equal to twice a sloping side, and **R = y/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **R = y/2 marks EVERY economical section** — rectangle (b = 2y), trapezoid, and semicircle. Use it as an instant check. In practice, though, the side slope is fixed by **soil stability** (1:1 firm earth, 2:1 loose sand), and the section is optimised within that constraint.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is not correct for the heading and benching method of tunnelling?
options: Drilling and mucking can be done simultaneously
Benching provides a platform for working on the heading
Removal of muck from the heading is very easy
questions.solution:
**"Removal of muck from the heading is very easy" is the incorrect statement.**

In the heading and benching method the tunnel face is driven in two parts: the **heading** is the upper portion, advanced first, and the **bench** is the lower portion, excavated afterwards. The bench is left standing so that it forms a working platform from which the heading above can be drilled and supported.

What is genuinely true of the method:
- **Drilling and mucking proceed simultaneously** — the heading can be drilled while the bench below is being mucked out, which is the method's main attraction.
- **The bench provides the platform** for working on the heading, so no separate staging is needed.

What is **not** true is that mucking from the heading is easy. The heading is elevated above the tunnel invert, so the broken rock must be dropped or cast down to the bench level before it can be loaded and hauled out. That double handling makes muck removal from the heading **awkward and slow** — one of the recognised drawbacks of the method, not an advantage.

Other tunnelling methods for comparison: full-face (small tunnels in sound rock), drift, and the New Austrian Tunnelling Method.

examTip.trap: Another **NOT** question — underline it. Three statements will be correct advantages and one will be false.
examTip.trick: In tunnelling, muck removal from the heading is one of the **harder** logistical problems, not an easy one: the working face is confined, access is single-ended, and haulage governs the cycle time.
examTip.mnemonic: **Muck disposal usually CONTROLS the advance rate** in a tunnel, along with ventilation and support installation. Any statement calling it easy deserves suspicion.

questions.stem: Which of the following rollers is used to compact coarse grained soil?
questions.solution:
**Vibratory roller.**

Coarse-grained soils — sands and gravels — are compacted by **rearranging particles into a denser packing**, and vibration is by far the most effective way to do that. The oscillating drum momentarily reduces inter-particle friction, letting grains slip into the voids, and the air is driven out. Static weight alone is comparatively ineffective in granular material.

Match each roller to the soil it suits, since this is asked both ways round:

| Roller | Action | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Vibratory** | **Dynamic — vibration** | **Coarse-grained: sand, gravel, rockfill** |
| Sheep-foot / tamping | Kneading + static weight | **Clay and silty clay** |
| Pneumatic tyred | Kneading, static | Both fine-grained and non-cohesive; also bituminous layers |
| Smooth wheel (static) | Static weight | Finishing, proof rolling, asphalt surfacing |

The underlying principle: **cohesive soils need kneading and manipulation, cohesionless soils need vibration.** That single sentence answers most compaction-equipment questions.

examTip.trick: Match the roller to the soil: **vibratory/smooth wheel** for **coarse-grained** (vibration rearranges grains into a denser packing), **sheepsfoot** for **cohesive** clay (the feet knead and remould it), **pneumatic** for a wide range, **smooth wheel** for finishing bituminous surfaces.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vibration works on sand, kneading works on clay.** Vibrating a clay achieves little, because the water cannot escape quickly — which is the same compaction-versus-consolidation distinction that runs through soil mechanics.

questions.stem: What is included in an impact assessment?
options: A detailed assessment of the planned project and selected alternatives compared to the baseline conditions
Qualitative descriptions measuring high, medium and low impacts
Quantitative descriptions such as indicating cubic metres of water withdrawn, sewage produced and pollutants released
All the data collection, analysis and developed plans summarised in a well-structured and concise document
questions.solution:
**All the data collection, analysis and developed plans summarised in a well-structured, concise document.**

The three earlier options are each only one *component* of an impact assessment; option (d) describes the assessment as a whole — the compiled report that gathers the baseline study, the qualitative and quantitative impact predictions, and the mitigation plans into a document that stakeholders and decision-makers can actually act on.

The environmental assessment tiers under Nepal's Environment Protection Act, in increasing order of depth:

| Level | When required |
|---|---|
| **BES** (Brief Environmental Study) | Small projects with minor impacts |
| **IEE** (Initial Environmental Examination) | Moderate impacts; scoping not always needed |
| **EIA** (Environmental Impact Assessment) | Major projects with significant impacts; full scoping, ToR approval and public hearing |

The standard EIA sequence: screening → scoping and Terms of Reference → baseline data collection → impact prediction and evaluation → **mitigation measures** → environmental management plan → monitoring and auditing, with **public consultation** running through it.

The key idea to hold on to: an impact assessment is not merely a list of impacts but a **decision-support document**, which is why the answer is the option describing the whole compiled report.

examTip.trick: A report is a **communication** document, not a filing cabinet. Its purpose is to let a decision-maker who was not involved understand the work and act on it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Well structured and concise are both load-bearing words.** A report that contains everything but cannot be navigated has failed. Standard order: summary, introduction, methodology, findings, analysis, conclusions, recommendations, appendices — with the **raw data in the appendix**, never in the body.

questions.stem: Consolidation settlement occurs due to:
questions.solution:
**Expulsion of water from the voids.**

Consolidation is defined for a **saturated** soil. When load is applied, it is carried at first entirely by the pore water as excess pore pressure. As that water is slowly squeezed out, the excess pressure dissipates and the load transfers to the soil skeleton — effective stress rises and the soil compresses.
