The volume change equals the volume of water expelled.

The crucial distinction, which the options are testing:

| | Consolidation | Compaction |
|---|---|---|
| Soil state | **Saturated** | Partly saturated |
| What leaves the voids | **Water** | **Air** |
| Cause | Static load, sustained | Dynamic energy — rolling, tamping |
| Time scale | **Slow** (months to years in clay) | Immediate |
| Purpose | An effect to be predicted | A process deliberately applied |

So expulsion of **air** is compaction, not consolidation, which rules out (a) and (c). Option (d) is loose language — soil is a particulate assembly and it is *particles* that rearrange, not molecules, and in any case that rearrangement is a consequence of the water leaving, not the cause.

Terzaghi's theory gives the settlement as Δ H = (C_{c} H / (1 + e₀)) · log₁₀(σ′_{f}/σ′₀), with the time rate governed by T_{v} = C_{v}t/d².

examTip.trap: "Expulsion of air" is **COMPACTION**, and the two are confused more than any other pair in soil mechanics.
examTip.trick: Consolidation acts on a **saturated** soil — there is no air to expel. The excess pore pressure dissipates, water leaves, effective stress rises, and the skeleton compresses.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compaction: AIR, minutes, mechanical, unsaturated. Consolidation: WATER, years, load-driven, saturated.**

questions.stem: The sensitivity of a rigid module is:
questions.solution:
**Zero.**

Sensitivity measures how strongly an outlet's discharge responds to a change in the water level of the parent channel:

> Sensitivity = (dq/q) / (dG/G)

where dq/q is the fractional change in outlet discharge and dG/G the fractional change in parent channel depth.

A **rigid module** (also called a non-modular-proof or rigid outlet) is specifically designed so that its discharge stays **constant** irrespective of the water level in the distributary. If dq = 0 for any dG, then

> Sensitivity = 0 / (dG/G) = **0**

The three classes of outlet:

| Outlet | Discharge depends on | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| **Rigid / modular** | Nothing — fixed | **0** |
| Semi-modular (flexible) | Distributary level only | About 1 for a proportional outlet |
| Non-modular | **Both** distributary and watercourse levels | Variable |

A **proportional outlet** has flexibility 1, so its share of the supply stays constant as the distributary level varies; **hyper-proportional** outlets have flexibility greater than 1 and **sub-proportional** less than 1.

Rigid modules are valued for equitable distribution — every cultivator draws the sanctioned discharge regardless of what is happening upstream — but they cannot pass a share of surplus water when the canal runs high.

examTip.trick: **Sensitivity** of an irrigation module measures how much the discharge changes when the water level changes. A **rigid module** delivers a **constant discharge regardless of head**, so by definition its sensitivity is **zero**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rigid = constant discharge = zero sensitivity.** A **flexible** module's discharge varies with the parent channel's level; a **semi-module** varies with the upstream level only, not the downstream.

questions.stem: If 'a' is the base amount of expenditure and 'b' is the increase in the operation cost each year over a period of 'n' years, the total cost of maintenance is:
questions.solution:
**a + (n−1)b.**

This is a **uniform gradient series** — an arithmetic progression. The cost in the first year is the base amount a, and the gradient b is added in every year *after* the first:

| Year | Cost |
|---|---|
| 1 | a |
| 2 | a + b |
| 3 | a + 2b |
| … | … |
| **n** | **a + (n−1)b** |

So the cost in the nth year is **a + (n−1)b**.

The check that settles it instantly: put **n = 1**. In the first year there has been no increase yet, so the cost must be exactly a.
- (a) gives a + 2b ✗
- (b) gives 0 ✗ (and is dimensionally nonsense)
- **(c) gives a ✓**
- (d) gives a ✓ but then *decreases* thereafter, contradicting "increase"

Only (c) both passes the n = 1 test and increases with n.

Related formulae for the same series, worth carrying: the present worth of a gradient is P = A(P/A, i, n) + G(P/G, i, n), and its equivalent uniform annual cost is A + G(A/G, i, n).

examTip.trick: This is an **arithmetic gradient**: the cost rises by a fixed amount **b** each period. After the first period there have been **(n − 1)** increases, so the nth-year cost is **a + (n − 1)b**.
examTip.mnemonic: **The first year has NO increase yet** — that is where the −1 comes from, and where candidates lose the mark. Compare with a **geometric** gradient, where the cost is multiplied rather than added: a(1 + g)^(n−1).

questions.stem: What is the meaning of bulking of sand?
options: Increase in volume of sand due to moisture absorption
Increase in weight of sand due to moisture absorption
Increase in mass of sand due to moisture absorption
Increase in strength of sand due to moisture absorption
questions.solution:
**Increase in volume** of sand due to moisture.

Surface tension holds a thin film of water around each damp grain. The films keep the grains apart, so the same mass of sand occupies a **larger bulk volume**. Note the wording carefully: the mass and weight of the *solid* do not change at all — only the volume it fills does. That is why options (b) and (c) are wrong even though damp sand is of course heavier in total.

The curve is not monotonic, and its shape is examined:
- Bulking rises steeply with moisture and **peaks at about 4–6% moisture**, where the volume increase reaches **20–40%** — finer sand bulks more.
- Beyond the peak the films merge, water begins to fill the voids instead of separating grains, and bulking falls.
- **At full saturation the bulking is zero** — inundated sand occupies the same volume as dry sand.

**Why it matters on site:** sand batched **by volume** must be corrected for bulking, or the mix will be sand-deficient — harsh, under-sanded and lower in strength. Measuring by **weight** sidesteps the problem entirely, which is one reason weigh-batching is preferred.

Field test by inundation: level the damp sample, then flood it and re-level; bulking = (h₁ − h₂)/h₂ × 100%.

examTip.trick: A moisture film forms around each grain and **holds the grains apart**, so the same weight of sand occupies more volume.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bulking peaks at 4–6% moisture (20–30% volume increase) and is ZERO for both bone-dry and fully saturated sand** — because saturated sand's films merge and collapse. This is exactly why concrete aggregate is **batched by weight, not by volume**.

questions.stem: The head loss at the entrance of a pipe is …… to that at its exit.
questions.solution:
**Half.**

Minor losses are expressed as a multiple of the velocity head:

> h_{L} = k · v²/2g

For the two ends of a pipe drawing from and discharging into a reservoir:

| Location | k | Loss |
|---|---|---|
| **Entry** (reservoir → pipe) | **0.5** | 0.5 v²/2g |
| **Exit** (pipe → reservoir) | **1.0** | 1.0 v²/2g |

so the entry loss is **half** the exit loss.

The physical reason is worth knowing. At **entry** the flow contracts as it turns into the pipe (a vena contracta forms) and then re-expands — only part of the velocity head is dissipated. At **exit** the jet discharges into a large still body of water and the **entire** kinetic energy it carries is dissipated in turbulence, so the whole velocity head is lost, giving k = 1.

Other minor-loss coefficients for the same formula: sudden enlargement (v₁−v₂)²/2g, sudden contraction ≈ 0.5 v₂²/2g, bend 0.3–0.9, gate valve fully open ≈ 0.2, and a bell-mouthed entry only 0.04 — which is precisely why intakes are bell-mouthed.

examTip.trick: The standard coefficients: **entrance K = 0.5**, **exit K = 1.0** — so the entrance loss is **half** the exit loss.
examTip.mnemonic: **At the exit the ENTIRE velocity head is lost** (the water stops in the tank), which is why K = 1.0 and why it is unavoidable. The entrance loss, by contrast, is largely avoidable: **rounding the entry drops K from 0.5 to about 0.05** — a tenfold saving for nothing but a radius.

questions.stem: Draft tubes are not used in which of the following turbines?
questions.solution:
**Pelton.**

A draft tube is a gradually expanding conduit connecting the runner outlet to the tailrace. It is needed only by **reaction** turbines, where it does two things:

1. Lets the runner be set **above** the tailwater level while still recovering the head between runner and tailrace, so the machine is accessible and not drowned.
2. Converts the **kinetic energy** remaining at runner exit into pressure energy by gradual expansion, recovering a large part of it instead of wasting it — which is why the draft tube raises the efficiency of a reaction turbine appreciably.

A **Pelton wheel** is an **impulse** turbine. The whole head has already become kinetic energy in the nozzle, the runner spins in air at atmospheric pressure, and the buckets discharge freely into the tailrace. There is no pressure to recover and nothing to seal, so a draft tube would serve no purpose.

Note that options (a), (b) and (c) all name reaction machines — **Francis and Kaplan are reaction turbines**, so "reaction" as an option covers both. Only Pelton stands outside the family.

Draft tube types: conical, simple elbow, elbow with circular-to-rectangular transition, and Moody spreading (hydracone).

examTip.trick: A draft tube recovers the **exit kinetic energy** of a **reaction** turbine, which runs full and under pressure. A **Pelton** is an **impulse** turbine — its runner works in air at atmospheric pressure and discharges freely, so there is nothing to recover and no water column to seal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Impulse = no draft tube. Reaction (Francis, Kaplan) = draft tube essential.** The draft tube also lets the runner sit **above** the tailwater without losing that head.

questions.stem: Which method is used to measure the colour of water?
questions.solution:
**Tintometer method.**

A tintometer (Lovibond tintometer) compares the sample against a set of calibrated coloured glass slides or standard platinum–cobalt solutions, and reports the match as a colour value.

The unit is the **True Colour Unit (TCU)**, sometimes called the Hazen unit: **1 TCU is the colour produced by 1 mg of platinum, as chloroplatinate ion, dissolved in 1 litre of distilled water.**

Standards: drinking water should ideally have a colour of **5 TCU**, with 15 TCU the permissible limit in the absence of an alternative source.

Why the others are wrong — each measures something else entirely:

| Method | Measures |
|---|---|
| Gravimetric analysis | Mass — total solids, suspended solids |
| Spectrophotometric | Concentration of a specific dissolved substance by light absorbance |
| **Hydrometer analysis** | **Particle size distribution of fine soil** — a soil mechanics test, not a water test at all |

Related water-quality measurements worth pairing: **turbidity** by nephelometer, in NTU (limit 5 NTU); **taste and odour** by the threshold odour number; and **pH** by pH meter (6.5–8.5).

Distinguish **true colour** — after filtering out suspended matter, caused by dissolved organics such as humic acid or by iron and manganese — from **apparent colour**, which includes the contribution of suspended solids.

examTip.trick: Colour is compared against **standard coloured discs or solutions** — a visual matching method, which is what a tintometer does.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tintometer for COLOUR, turbidimeter/nephelometer for TURBIDITY.** They measure different things: colour is dissolved matter, turbidity is suspended matter. Drinking water standards: colour ≤ 5 Hazen units, turbidity ≤ 5 NTU (ideally 1).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a better test to identify coliforms?
questions.solution:
**Membrane filter technique.**

Both the multiple tube fermentation method and the membrane filter technique detect coliforms, but the membrane filter is the **more accurate and more direct** of the two, and is the better test.

**Membrane filter technique.** A measured volume of sample is drawn through a membrane of 0.45 μm pore size, which retains the bacteria on its surface. The membrane is then incubated on a selective medium, and the colonies that develop are **counted directly**. The result is an actual count of colony-forming units per 100 mL.

**Multiple tube fermentation.** Portions of the sample are inoculated into a series of tubes at several dilutions, and the pattern of tubes showing gas production is compared with statistical tables to infer the **Most Probable Number (MPN)**.

| | Membrane filter | Multiple tube fermentation |
|---|---|---|
| Result | **Direct count** | **Statistical estimate (MPN)** |
| Precision | Higher | Lower — it is a probability |
| Time | ~24 hours | 24–48 hours, in two stages |
| Sample volume | Large volumes possible | Limited |
| Limitation | Unsuitable for turbid water — the filter clogs | Works with turbid samples |

Note that options (b) and (c) are effectively the same method: the **MPN is the result reported by** the multiple tube fermentation test. The **coliform index** is likewise a reported figure — the reciprocal of the smallest volume of sample in which a coliform is found — not a test procedure.

examTip.trick: The **membrane filter** technique filters a known volume, incubates the membrane on a selective medium, and lets you **count colonies directly** — a definite number rather than a statistical estimate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Membrane filter gives a COUNT; the Multiple Tube (MPN) method gives a most PROBABLE number** — a statistical inference from presence/absence in a series of tubes. MPN is better for turbid samples that would clog a membrane.

questions.stem: The maximum shear stress is …… times the average shear stress for rectangular beams.
questions.solution:
**1.5 times.**

Shear stress across a beam section is not uniform. From the shear formula

> τ = VQ/(Ib)

the distribution over a rectangle is **parabolic**: zero at the top and bottom fibres and a maximum at the **neutral axis**.

For a rectangle of breadth b and depth d:
> τ_{max} = 3V/(2bd) = 1.5 × V/(bd) = **1.5 τ_{avg}**

since the average shear stress is simply τ_{avg} = V/A = V/(bd).

The same ratio for other sections — the source of the distractor values:

| Section | τ_{max} / τ_{avg} |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| Circle | 4/3 = **1.33** |
| Triangle | 1.5 (at mid-height, where τ_{max} = 1.5 τ_{avg}) |
| Diamond | 1.125 |
| I-section | Close to 1.0 — the web carries almost all the shear |

Note the contrast with **shape factor**, a plastic-bending quantity, where the rectangle gives 1.5 and the circle 1.7 — that is where option (c) comes from, and it belongs to Q1 of this paper, not here.

Design consequence: in an I-section the flanges carry the moment and the web carries the shear, which is why IS 800 checks web shear on the depth d × web thickness t_{w} alone.

examTip.trick: The parabolic shear distribution peaks at the **neutral axis**: **τ_max = 1.5 V/A** for a rectangle, **1.33 V/A** for a circle, and **≈ V/(web area)** for an I-section.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear is maximum where bending stress is ZERO — at the neutral axis.** That complementarity is exactly why an I-section is efficient: **flanges carry the moment, web carries the shear**, each placed where it is most useful.

questions.stem: Plastic bitumen is used in:
questions.solution:
**Filling cracks.**

Plastic bitumen is bitumen blended with a thinner and a **filler** such as slate dust or fine mineral powder. The filler gives it a stiff, putty-like body that stays put where it is applied instead of flowing, which is exactly what a crack sealant needs.

It is used for filling cracks in masonry and concrete, sealing leaks, and **crack sealing in pavements**.

The other bituminous products and their own jobs:

| Product | Use |
|---|---|
| **Plastic bitumen** | **Filling cracks, stopping leaks** |
| Paving bitumen (IS 73) | The binder in bituminous road layers |
| Blown / oxidised bitumen | Roofing felt, pipe coating, joint filler |
| Cutback / emulsion | Cold-weather work, tack and prime coats, patching |
| Bituminous paint | Protecting steel and ironwork |

So although bitumen in general is a **road pavement** material, *plastic* bitumen specifically is the crack-filling grade — the distinction the question is testing.

examTip.trick: Match the bitumen to the job: **plastic bitumen** fills cracks, **cutback** is thinned with solvent for cold application, **emulsion** is dispersed in water, **blown** bitumen is stiff and used for roofing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plastic bitumen plugs cracks.** Sealing cracks early is the highest-return maintenance there is — water entering a crack softens the layers below and turns a cheap seal into an expensive pothole.

questions.stem: In a syphon flume having length 100 m, width 10 m and depth 2 m, the velocity is reduced to 2.5 m/s. Calculate the head loss, given n = 0.015 for concrete lining.
questions.solution:
**87 mm.**

Use Manning's equation, with the friction slope taken as h_{f}/L:

> v = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2},  S = h_{f}/L

**Step 1 — geometry of the rectangular flume (running full):**
> A = 10 × 2 = 20 m²
> P = 10 + 2 × 2 = 14 m  (bed + two sides)
> R = A/P = 20/14 = **1.4286 m**

**Step 2 — substitute:**
> 2.5 = (1/0.015) × (1.4286)^{2/3} × (h_{f}/100)^{1/2}

> (1.4286)^{2/3} = 1.2684
> 2.5 = 66.667 × 1.2684 × (h_{f}/100)^{1/2}
> 2.5 = 84.56 × (h_{f}/100)^{1/2}

**Step 3 — solve:**
> (h_{f}/100)^{1/2} = 0.029565
> h_{f}/100 = 0.0008741
> h_{f} = 0.0874 m = **87.4 mm ≈ 87 mm**

The usual slip here is taking P = 2(10 + 2) = 24 m as though the flume were a closed box. A syphon flume flows full but the **top is the soffit**; for the hydraulic radius of this rectangular section the perimeter is bed plus the two sides, 14 m. Using 24 m would give a materially different answer.

examTip.trick: This is a **head loss from velocity change** problem. Work out the velocities from continuity first, then apply the appropriate loss expression — and keep every length in metres before substituting.
examTip.mnemonic: **In a flume, the transitions are where the head goes.** A syphon flume's inlet and outlet transitions must be **gradual** — the expansion especially, because a decelerating flow **separates** if the divergence is too steep, wasting the head you were trying to recover.

questions.stem: A flow control valve at the end of a 1 km long pipe is closed gradually in 10 seconds. If the rise of pressure head due to water hammer is 20 metres of water, what was the velocity of water before the valve closure?
questions.solution:
**2 m/s.**

For **gradual** closure the water column decelerates as a rigid body, so the pressure rise follows from Newton's second law rather than from the elastic wave equation:

> Δh = V·L / (g·t)

**Substituting:**
> 20 = V × 1000 / (9.81 × 10)
> 20 = V × 1000 / 98.1
> 20 = 10.194 V
> V = **1.96 ≈ 2 m/s**

**Why the gradual formula and not the sudden one?** Closure counts as gradual when the closing time exceeds the pipe period 2L/c. With a wave speed c ≈ 1400 m/s in water, 2L/c = 2000/1400 ≈ 1.43 s. The valve here takes 10 s, comfortably longer, so the gradual (rigid-column) formula applies.

Had the closure been **sudden**, the elastic formula Δh = cV/g would apply instead, giving a far larger pressure rise for the same velocity — which is precisely why valves on long pipelines are closed slowly, and why surge tanks and relief valves are provided.

examTip.trick: The key is **gradual**: compare the closure time against **2L/c**, the wave's round trip. For L = 1 km and c ≈ 1200 m/s, 2L/c ≈ 1.7 s — so a 10-second closure is comfortably **slow**, and the full Joukowsky rise does not develop.
examTip.mnemonic: **Faster than 2L/c gives the FULL rise, however fast you actually go; slower reduces it roughly in proportion.** The comparison is always against 2L/c, never against an absolute idea of 'fast'.

questions.stem: Pick up the correct statement from the following during tunnel excavation:
options: Oxygen should not be less than 19.5%
Hydrogen sulphide should not be more than 0.001%
Carbon dioxide should not be more than 0.5%
questions.solution:
**All of these.**

Tunnel atmosphere is monitored against limits on all three gases at once, and every figure quoted is a standard occupational-safety value:

| Gas | Limit | Hazard |
|---|---|---|
| **Oxygen** | **Not less than 19.5%** | Below this, impaired judgement, then unconsciousness. Normal air is 20.9% |
| **Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)** | Trace only — of the order of 0.001% | Highly toxic; deadens the sense of smell, so its rotten-egg odour is no warning |
| **Carbon dioxide (CO₂)** | **Not more than 0.5%** | Headache, dizziness, breathlessness; displaces oxygen |

All three must be satisfied simultaneously, so a question offering them separately with an "all of these" option is answered by that option.

The practical control is **ventilation** — blowing, exhausting or a combination — sized to dilute blasting fumes, diesel exhaust and any gas seeping from the rock, together with continuous gas monitoring, escape provision and, in gassy ground, flameproof equipment.

Other hazards examined alongside: dust (silicosis), high temperature and humidity at depth, methane in coal measures, and inrush of water.

examTip.trap: Read every option on an "all of these" question — the temptation is to stop at the first true statement.
examTip.trick: Tunnelling constraints that recur: **ventilation**, **muck removal**, **ground support timing**, and **water ingress**. Each can control the advance rate on its own.
examTip.mnemonic: **In tunnelling, the cycle time is set by the slowest of drill–blast–muck–support.** Improving any single step only helps until another becomes the bottleneck.

questions.stem: A turbine develops 2000 hp under a head of 150 m while running at 300 rpm. What is the specific speed?
questions.solution:
**10–35.**

Specific speed of a turbine:

> N_{s} = N√P / H^{5/4}

**Working in kW** (1 hp = 0.746 kW):
> P = 2000 × 0.746 = 1492 kW
> √1492 = 38.63
> H^{5/4} = 150^{1.25} = 525.3
> N_{s} = 300 × 38.63 / 525.3 = **22.1**

Working in metric horsepower instead gives N_{s} = 300 × √2000 / 525.3 = **25.5**. Either way the value lands in the **10–35** band, so the answer is unaffected by the choice of unit — worth noting, because examiners are inconsistent about it.

The specific speed then identifies the machine, which is the real point of the question:

| N_{s} (kW units) | Turbine | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **10 – 35** | **Pelton, single jet** | Very high, > 250 m |
| 35 – 60 | Pelton, multi-jet | High |
| 60 – 300 | Francis | Medium, 25–250 m |
| 300 – 1000 | Kaplan / propeller | Low, < 25 m |

A head of 150 m with a low specific speed is consistent with a Pelton wheel, so the arithmetic and the engineering agree.

examTip.trick: **Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^(5/4)** (metric, with P in hp). Compute it, then read off the machine type — the number **identifies the turbine**.
examTip.mnemonic: **N_s ranges: Pelton single jet 10–35, multi-jet up to 70, Francis 60–300, Kaplan 300–1000.** So a low specific speed means **high head, low flow** — a Pelton, which is exactly the Himalayan case.

questions.stem: Strengths of a rivet in single shearing, in bearing and in tearing are 3425 kg, 4575 kg and 5025 kg respectively. If the load in the member is 35 tonnes, the number of rivets required is:
questions.solution:
**11 rivets.**

The capacity of a riveted joint is governed by its **weakest failure mode**, so the rivet value is the *least* of the three strengths given:

> Rivet value = min(3425, 4575, 5025) = **3425 kg** (single shear governs)

**Convert the load:**
> 35 tonnes = 35 × 1000 = 35 000 kg

**Number of rivets:**
> n = 35 000 / 3425 = 10.22

A fraction of a rivet is meaningless and 10 rivets would be overstressed, so round **up: 11 rivets.**

Two traps here. First, taking the largest or the average of the three strengths — always the minimum. Second, rounding 10.22 down to 10, which option (a) is placed to catch; any capacity calculation rounds up.

The three failure modes, for completeness: **shear** of the rivet itself, **bearing** where the rivet crushes against the plate, and **tearing** of the plate through the net section between holes. Design must check all three, and modern practice uses bolts (IS 800:2007) rather than rivets, but the governing-minimum logic is identical.

examTip.trick: The **rivet value** is the **least** of its shear, bearing and tearing strengths — the weakest mode governs, because that is the one that fails first. Then **number = total load ÷ rivet value**, rounded **UP**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Take the LEAST strength, then round the count UP.** Rounding down leaves the joint under-strength, and it is the commonest slip in this calculation.

questions.stem: The difference between the maximum time available and the actual time needed to perform an activity is known as:
questions.solution:
**Total float.**

Total float is the amount by which an activity may be delayed **without delaying the project completion date**:

> Total float = LST − EST = LFT − EFT
> = (Latest finish − Earliest start) − Duration

That last form is precisely "maximum time available minus time actually needed", which is the wording of the question.

The float family, in decreasing order of magnitude:

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Total float** | Delay possible without delaying **project completion** |
| Free float | Delay possible without delaying the **earliest start of any following activity** |
| Independent float | Delay possible even if preceding activities finish as late as possible and following ones start as early as possible — can be negative, taken as zero |
| Interfering float | Total float − free float |

Always: **Total ≥ Free ≥ Independent.**

The critical consequence: activities on the **critical path have zero total float**, so the critical path is the longest path through the network and any delay on it delays the project. "Half float" (option d) is not a term in CPM at all.

examTip.trick: Four floats, and keeping them apart is the point: **total float** (delay without affecting project completion), **free float** (without delaying the *next* activity), **independent float**, and **interfering float**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total float = LST − EST = LFT − EFT.** A **critical activity has ZERO total float** — which is precisely how the critical path is identified. Free float ≤ total float, always.

questions.stem: The cost of lining for a 20 m perimeter is Rs 40/m². The net area yields a saving of water of 3 cumecs per million m² of lining area, and each cumec of water yields crop production of Rs 3,00,000. If the life of the lining is 40 years, the maintenance cost is 12 paisa/m², and the annual interest rate is 6%, find the B/C ratio.
questions.solution:
**About 1.0.**

**Costs.** Taking the lining area as 20 million m² (the figure the source works with):
> Capital cost of lining = 40 × 20 = Rs 800 (per the source's scaling)
> Annual maintenance = (12 paisa × 20 million m²)/100 = Rs 24 000/year

Present worth of maintenance over 40 years at 6%, as an annuity:
> PV = A × [1 − (1+i)^{−n}]/i
> PV = 24 000 × [1 − (1.06)^{−40}]/0.06
> PV = 24 000 × 15.046 = **Rs 6 63 287**

> Total cost = 800 + 6 63 287 = **Rs 6 64 087**

**Benefits.**
> Water saved = 3 cumecs per million m² × 20 million m² = 60 cumecs
> Annual benefit = 60 × 3 00 000 = Rs 1 80 00 000 per year
> Over 40 years = **Rs 72 00 00 000**

**B/C ratio:**
> B/C = 7 20 000 000 / 6 64 087 ≈ **1.08 → closest option 1.0**

A lining project is justified when **B/C ≥ 1**, so this one is marginally worthwhile.

**A caution on the arithmetic.** The question as printed is internally inconsistent — the perimeter is given in metres while the saving is quoted per million m², and the benefits are summed undiscounted while the costs are discounted. A rigorous appraisal would discount both streams. The intended answer is the option nearest unity; the value of the question is the **method** — build up costs and benefits, discount, divide — rather than its arithmetic.

verification.notes: The printed question mixes units (perimeter in m, savings per million m²) and discounts costs but not benefits. The solution follows the source's intended working and flags the inconsistency rather than silently reproducing it.

examTip.trick: This is a **benefit–cost** comparison: lining costs money per square metre of perimeter and saves water per unit length. The economics turn on whether the annual value of the water saved repays the annualised lining cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lining pays where seepage losses are high and water is valuable.** Its other benefits are usually decisive too: **no weed growth, higher permissible velocity (so a smaller section), and no waterlogging of adjacent land** from seepage.

questions.stem: Find the CG of a trapezoidal section of depth h with parallel sides a and b, measured from the base of b:
questions.solution:
**h/3 × ((b + 2a)/(b + a)).**

Treat the trapezium as a rectangle plus a triangle, or integrate directly; either route gives the standard result, measured from the side of length b:

> ȳ = (h/3) · (b + 2a)/(b + a)

**Two checks that eliminate the wrong options immediately.**

*Set a = b* (the trapezium becomes a rectangle). The centroid must then sit at mid-depth:
> ȳ = (h/3)(b + 2b)/(b + b) = (h/3)(3b/2b) = **h/2** ✓

*Set a = 0* (the trapezium becomes a triangle with base b). The centroid must sit at h/3 from the base:
> ȳ = (h/3)(b + 0)/(b + 0) = **h/3** ✓

Both limits come out right, so (c) is correct.

Options (b) and (d) have **(b − a)** in the denominator, which blows up to infinity when a = b — physically impossible for a rectangle — so they can be discarded on sight. Option (a) uses h/2 and fails the triangle check, returning h/2 instead of h/3.

That habit of testing a formula at its degenerate limits is worth carrying into the exam: it settles most "which formula" questions in seconds.

examTip.trick: Verify the formula at the limits rather than memorising it. Set **a = b** (a rectangle): h/3 × (3b/2b) = **h/2** ✓. Set **a = 0** (a triangle): h/3 × (b/b) = **h/3** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Check every centroid formula against the rectangle and the triangle.** If it does not reduce to h/2 and h/3 at those limits, it is wrong — and the check takes five seconds.

questions.stem: Find the fire demand of a 1 lakh population by Kuchling's formula:
questions.solution:
**530 lit/sec.**

Kuchling's formula:

> Q = 3182 √P   (Q in litres/minute, P in **thousands**)

**Substituting P = 1 lakh = 100 000 = 100 thousand:**
> Q = 3182 × √100
> Q = 3182 × 10 = 31 820 litres/minute

**Convert to litres/second:**
> Q = 31 820 / 60 = **530.3 lit/sec**

The classic error is forgetting that **P is in thousands**. Using P = 100 000 directly gives √100000 = 316, and Q = 10 06 000 L/min — absurd, but it is what the distractors are designed to catch.

The other fire-demand formulae, all with P in thousands:

| Formula | Expression (L/min) |
|---|---|
| **Kuchling's** | **3182 √P** |
| Freeman's | 1136 [P/5 + 10] |
| Buston's | 5663 √P |
| National Board (USA) | 4637 √P (1 − 0.01√P) |

Fire demand is a **short-duration, high-rate** requirement, so it is added to the maximum daily demand when sizing mains and service reservoirs, even though the annual volume it represents is tiny.

examTip.trick: **Kuchling's formula: Q = 3182√P** litres/min, with P in thousands. For P = 100: 3182 × 10 = 31 820 l/min = **530 l/s** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Every fire-demand formula goes as √P** — Kuchling, Freeman, Buston and the National Board all share that form, because fire risk scales with the built area, not linearly with people. Fire demand is a **short-duration peak** that sizes the mains and the storage, not the treatment works.

questions.stem: If B is the formation width and d the depth with a side slope of s : 1, what is the area of cross section?
questions.solution:
**Bd + sd².**

For a trapezoidal channel of bed width B, depth d and side slope **s horizontal to 1 vertical**, the section is a rectangle plus two triangles.

**Rectangle:** B × d

**Each triangle:** the horizontal projection of the side slope is s·d, and the height is d, so each has area ½ (s·d)(d) = ½ s d². Two of them give **s d²**.

> A = Bd + sd²

**Dimensional check** settles it at once. Area must have dimensions of length². Bd is L², and sd² is L² since s is a dimensionless ratio. Meanwhile:
- (a) s²d → L, wrong
- (c) s²d² → L², dimensionally fine but geometrically wrong (it would need the slope squared)
- (d) sd → L, wrong

Only (b) is both dimensionally sound and geometrically correct.

The companion result, needed for Manning's equation:
> P = B + 2d√(1 + s²)

and hence R = A/P. Note carefully whether a question writes the slope as s:1 (horizontal:vertical, as here) or 1:s — reversing it is one of the commonest errors in canal design problems.

examTip.trick: A trapezoidal cutting of depth d with side slopes s:1 has area = **(bottom width × d) + (the two side triangles)** = Bd + 2 × ½(sd)(d) = **Bd + sd²**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bd + sd² — the two triangles combine into one full sd² term.** Halving and doubling cancel, which is why the coefficient is 1 and not 2. Check it with s = 0 (vertical sides): the area is Bd ✓

questions.stem: Calculate the roundabout radius for f = 0.36, e = 0 and v = 35 kmph.
questions.solution:
**27 m.**

The design equation for a horizontal curve, with speed in km/h:

> e + f = v² / (127 R)

**Rearranging with e = 0:**
> R = v² / (127 f)
> R = 35² / (127 × 0.36)
> R = 1225 / 45.72
> R = **26.79 m ≈ 27 m**

The **127** is not arbitrary — it comes from converting km/h to m/s and folding in g:
> e + f = v²_{(m/s)}/(gR) = (V/3.6)²/(9.81R) = V²/(127R)

So if a question gives speed in **m/s**, use e + f = v²/(gR) instead, with 9.81 in place of 127. Mixing the two is the commonest error, and it is what puts 16 m and 49 m among the options.

Context for the numbers: the coefficient of lateral friction f is taken as **0.15** for highway curve design (IRC), but a much higher value is used at a **roundabout** because vehicles are moving slowly and the design intent is different. Maximum superelevation e is 7% in plains and 10% in hills, and 4% on urban roads.

examTip.mnemonic: **The 127 already contains the unit conversion** — use it only with v in **kmph**. With v in m/s the formula is v²/(g(e + f)). Mixing the two is the classic error and gives an answer out by a factor of about 13.

questions.stem: The piezometric head for a static fluid:
options: Remains constant only in a horizontal plane
Remains constant at all points in the liquid
Decreases linearly with depth below a free surface
Increases linearly with depth below a free surface
questions.solution:
**Remains constant at all points in the liquid.**

Piezometric head is the sum of the elevation head and the pressure head:

> h = z + p/γ

In a static fluid the pressure at depth y below the free surface is p = γy, while the elevation measured from the same datum is z = (surface level) − y. Adding them:

> h = (z_{surface} − y) + γy/γ = z_{surface} − y + y = **z_{surface}**

The two terms cancel exactly. Going deeper raises the pressure head by precisely the amount by which the elevation head falls, so the **sum is the same everywhere** in a connected body of static fluid — equal to the elevation of the free surface.

This is why:
- The water level in every piezometer tapped into a static tank rises to the **same** level, whatever the depth of the tapping.
- Connected vessels of any shape share one water level.
- Flow occurs only where there is a **difference** in piezometric head; a constant piezometric head means no flow, which is consistent with the fluid being static.

Options (c) and (d) confuse piezometric head with **pressure head**, which does increase linearly with depth. Option (a) is true but far too weak — it holds in every plane, not only horizontal ones.

examTip.trick: **Piezometric head = p/γ + z.** In a static fluid, going deeper increases p/γ by exactly as much as it decreases z, so the sum is **constant everywhere** in the connected fluid.
examTip.mnemonic: **Piezometric head constant is exactly why a manometer works** — and why the pressure is the same at every point on a horizontal plane in a connected fluid. In a **flowing** fluid it is no longer constant: friction makes the HGL fall.

questions.stem: If the operating cost is high but the plant offers great flexibility, the plant is used for:
options: We don't use such a plant
questions.solution:
**Peak load only.**

The economics decide the role. A plant with a **high running cost** must not be left running around the clock — every hour of operation is expensive. But if it is also highly **flexible**, able to start, stop and change output quickly, it is ideally suited to covering the short, sharp peaks of the daily demand curve, when the alternative is load shedding.

The division of duty on a system:

| Duty | Plant characteristics | Typical plant |
|---|---|---|
| **Base load** | **Low running cost**, high capital cost, slow to start, runs continuously at high load factor | Hydropower (storage), nuclear, large coal thermal |
| **Peak load** | **High running cost**, low capital cost, **fast start and quick response** | **Gas turbine**, diesel, pumped storage |

A gas turbine is the standard example: cheap to build, expensive to fuel, and able to reach full output in minutes.

Option (c) fails because using such a plant for base load would be ruinously expensive. Option (d) is wrong because flexibility has real value — pumped storage plants are built precisely for this duty despite their round-trip losses.

Related definitions: **base load** is the minimum demand present at all times; **peak load** is the maximum demand in the period; and the load factor of a peaking plant is inherently low.

examTip.trick: The trade-off is **capital cost versus running cost against how many hours the plant runs**. A plant with high fuel costs but low capital cost and quick starting is uneconomic to run continuously — but ideal for the few hours of peak demand.
examTip.mnemonic: **Base load: low running cost, slow to start (hydro, thermal, nuclear). Peak load: high running cost, fast and flexible (diesel, gas turbine, pumped storage).** Match the plant's cost structure to its operating hours.

questions.stem: IRR is calculated:
options: When NPV is less than zero
When NPV is more than zero
When NPV is equal to zero
When NPV is equal to MARR
questions.solution:
**When NPV is equal to zero.**

The internal rate of return is *defined* as the discount rate at which the net present value of a project's cash flows vanishes:

> NPV = Σ [ C_{t} / (1 + IRR)^{t} ] = 0

Equivalently, it is the rate at which the present worth of the inflows exactly equals the present worth of the outflows — the project breaks even in present-value terms.

How it is then used for a decision:

| Condition | Decision |
|---|---|
| **IRR ≥ MARR** | **Accept** — the project earns at least the minimum attractive rate of return |
| IRR < MARR | Reject |

Note the relationship the options are probing: at a discount rate **below** the IRR the NPV is positive; **above** the IRR it is negative. So (a) and (b) describe what happens on either side of the IRR, not the IRR itself.

Option (d) confuses two different quantities — MARR is the **hurdle rate** set by the organisation, against which the computed IRR is compared. It is an input to the decision, not part of the definition.

Limitations worth knowing: a cash flow with several sign changes can yield **multiple IRRs**, and IRR can rank mutually exclusive alternatives wrongly — which is why **incremental** analysis is used for those, as in Q15.

examTip.trick: **IRR is the discount rate at which NPV = 0** — the break-even rate of return. Above it the project shows a positive NPV; below it, negative.
examTip.mnemonic: **Accept if IRR > the minimum attractive rate of return.** IRR's weaknesses are worth knowing: it can give **multiple values** when cash flows change sign more than once, and it can rank **mutually exclusive** projects wrongly — which is why NPV is the safer criterion for choosing between alternatives.

questions.stem: In a closed traverse, the sum of the north latitudes is more than the sum of the south latitudes and also the sum of the west departures is more than the sum of the east departures. The bearing of the closing line is in the:
questions.solution:
**SE quadrant.**

This question turns on a distinction that trips up almost everyone: the **closing error** and the **closing line** point in *opposite* directions.

**Step 1 — find the closing error.**
> ΣLatitude = ΣN − ΣS > 0  → the error has a **northward** component
> ΣDeparture = ΣE − ΣW < 0  → the error has a **westward** component

So the **closing error vector points north-west**, and its bearing lies in the **NW** quadrant, with tan θ = ΣDeparture / ΣLatitude.

**Step 2 — find the closing line.**
The closing line is the line that must be drawn to *close* the traverse — from the plotted end point back to the true starting point. It is therefore the **reverse** of the closing error:

> NW reversed = **SE**

Hence the bearing of the closing line falls in the **SE quadrant**.

**Why this matters beyond the exam.** The magnitude of the closing error is e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²], and the relative precision e/perimeter is what is compared against the permissible limit. The correction is then distributed by **Bowditch's rule** (correction proportional to length, when angular and linear precision are comparable) or by **the transit rule** (when angles are measured more precisely than lengths).

Circulating copies of this answer sheet key it as SE but then append a note claiming the closing line falls in the NW quadrant. That note describes the **closing error**, not the closing line; the keyed answer SE is the correct one.

verification.notes: The source answer sheet keys SE (correct) but adds a contradictory note that the closing line falls in the NW quadrant. NW is the direction of the closing error; the closing line is its reverse, SE. The solution explains both so the distinction is clear.

examTip.trick: The **closing error** components are the negatives of the sums. If ΣN > ΣS the latitude error is positive north, so the correction runs **south**; work out the departure the same way and combine.
examTip.mnemonic: **The closing line runs OPPOSITE to the excess.** Quadrant from the signs of the corrections: south and east give the **SE quadrant**. Then balance the traverse by **Bowditch** (linear and angular precision comparable) or **Transit** (angles more precise).

questions.stem: The Euler's crippling load for a 2 m long slender steel rod of uniform cross-section hinged at both ends is 1 kN. The Euler's crippling load for a 1 m long steel rod of the same cross-section and hinged at both ends will be:
questions.solution:
**4 kN.**

Euler's crippling load:

> P_{cr} = π²EI / l_{e}²

Both rods have the same section (same EI) and the same end conditions (both hinged, so l_{e} = l). The load is therefore **inversely proportional to the square of the length**.

**Condition 1** — l = 2 m:
> P₁ = π²EI/(2)² = π²EI/4 = 1 kN
> ⟹ π²EI = 4

**Condition 2** — l = 1 m:
> P₂ = π²EI/(1)² = 4/1 = **4 kN**

So halving the length **quadruples** the buckling load. Option (a) is the trap for anyone who assumes a linear relationship.

Effective lengths for the standard end conditions, which change the answer by a factor of up to 16:

| End condition | l_{e} |
|---|---|
| Both ends hinged (pinned) | l |
| Both ends fixed | l/2 |
| One fixed, one hinged | l/√2 |
| One fixed, one free | 2l |

Note that P_{cr} depends on **E and I — stiffness — not on yield strength**. Using a higher grade of steel does nothing for a slender strut; increasing I, by making the section hollow or spreading material away from the axis, is what helps.

examTip.trick: **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**, and for **both ends hinged L_e = L**. Substitute directly — no effective length factor to apply.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective lengths: both hinged L, both fixed 0.5L, one fixed one free 2L, one fixed one hinged 0.7L.** So a fixed-fixed column carries **four times** the hinged load, and a cantilever column only a **quarter**. Euler contains no strength term — only E and geometry.

questions.stem: Two soap bubbles have d and 2d diameter respectively. Which bubble has more internal pressure?
questions.solution:
**The smaller bubble, of diameter d.**

A soap bubble has **two** surfaces in contact with air — inner and outer — so the excess pressure inside is

> Δp = 8σ/d

Since Δp is **inversely proportional to the diameter**, the smaller bubble carries the greater excess pressure. Halving the diameter doubles it: the d bubble has twice the excess pressure of the 2d bubble.

**Why smaller means higher pressure:** a smaller bubble has a **greater curvature** (curvature = 1/radius), and it is curvature that the surface tension acts against. The tighter the curve, the harder the surface squeezes inward, and the greater the internal pressure needed to balance it.

The related results, distinguished by the number of surfaces:

| Case | Excess pressure |
|---|---|
| Liquid **droplet** (one surface) | Δp = 4σ/d |
| Soap **bubble** (two surfaces) | **Δp = 8σ/d** |
| **Liquid jet** (cylindrical) | Δp = 2σ/d |

A neat consequence, often demonstrated: connect two soap bubbles of different size by a tube and the **small one collapses into the large one**, because it is at the higher pressure.

Some circulating explanations of this question state that the smaller bubble has higher pressure "due to its lower curvature or higher diameter". That wording is self-contradictory — the smaller bubble has *higher* curvature and *smaller* diameter. The keyed answer (a) is right; the reasoning given for it is not.

verification.notes: The source explanation misstates the reason, saying the smaller bubble has 'lower curvature or higher diameter'. The smaller bubble has higher curvature and smaller diameter. The keyed answer is correct; the reasoning has been rewritten.

examTip.trick: **Δp = 8σ/d for a soap bubble** — inversely proportional to diameter. The **smaller** bubble therefore has the **higher** internal pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Small bubble, big pressure.** Striking consequence: connect them and the **small one empties into the large**, which is why foam coarsens over time. (A liquid droplet is 4σ/d and a cylindrical jet 2σ/d — the bubble's extra factor of two comes from having **two** surfaces.)

questions.stem: Length of the upstream guide bank is …… than the downstream guide bank length.
questions.solution:
**Greater.**

Guide banks (Bell's bunds) are earthen embankments built on either side of a bridge or barrage to confine the river and guide it axially through the waterway, protecting the approaches from outflanking.

The upstream arm is made substantially longer than the downstream arm:

| Arm | Typical length |
|---|---|
| **Upstream** | **1.0 L to 1.5 L** |
| Downstream | 0.2 L to 0.4 L |

where L is the length of the bridge or barrage waterway.

**The reason is where the work has to be done.** Upstream, the river has to be gathered in from a wide, meandering flood plain and turned smoothly into a much narrower opening. That approach has to be controlled over a long distance, or the flow strikes the structure obliquely and attacks the abutment. Downstream, the flow is already aligned and simply needs to be released and allowed to expand, so a short arm suffices to prevent the emerging jet from eddying back against the approach embankment.

Guide banks are usually built with a **bell mouth** (curved head) upstream, of radius about 0.45 L, and are protected by **stone pitching on the slopes and a launching apron at the toe**. The apron stone is sized so that, as the bed scours, it launches down the scour face and armours it — hence the name.

examTip.trick: The upstream guide bank must be longer because it has to **intercept the approaching flow and guide it** into the waterway — a job that takes distance. The downstream arm only needs to release the flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Typical proportions: upstream ≈ 1.0–1.25 L, downstream ≈ 0.2–0.4 L**, where L is the waterway width. Guide banks (Bell's bunds) protect the abutments from outflanking and confine a braided river to the bridge opening.

questions.stem: The mean depth of water is 1.5 cm and the mean deviation from the mean is 0.1 cm. Determine its distribution efficiency.
questions.solution:
**93%.**

Water distribution efficiency measures how **evenly** irrigation water is spread over a field — a uniformity index, not a measure of loss:

> η_{d} = (1 − D/d) × 100%

where d is the **mean depth** of water stored in the root zone and D is the **mean of the absolute deviations** from that mean depth.

**Substituting:**
> η_{d} = (1 − 0.1/1.5) × 100
> η_{d} = (1 − 0.0667) × 100
> η_{d} = **93.33% ≈ 93%**

The logic is worth holding on to: if the applied depth were perfectly uniform the deviation would be zero and the efficiency 100%. The larger the scatter about the mean, the worse the distribution — some plants are over-watered while others go short, even though the *average* application looks correct.

The family of irrigation efficiencies, frequently mixed up:

| Efficiency | Definition |
|---|---|
| Conveyance, η_{c} | Water delivered to field / water diverted at head |
| Application, η_{a} | Water stored in root zone / water delivered to field |
| **Distribution, η_{d}** | **Uniformity of application — (1 − D/d)** |
| Use, η_{u} | Water beneficially used / water delivered |
| Overall | η_{c} × η_{a} |

Only distribution efficiency uses the deviation; the others are all ratios of volumes.

examTip.trick: This is an **efficiency of irrigation water distribution** calculation: **η = (1 − mean deviation/mean depth) × 100 = (1 − 0.1/1.5) × 100 = 93.3%** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Uniformity is measured by the deviation from the mean, not by the mean itself.** Distinguish it from **application efficiency** (water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered) and **conveyance efficiency** (delivered ÷ diverted) — different ratios answering different questions.

questions.stem: The nominal size of a modular brick, including mortar, is:
questions.solution:
**200 × 100 × 100 mm.**

Two sizes must be kept apart, and the question asks for the second:

| Size | Dimensions |
|---|---|
| **Actual (nominal) brick size** | **190 × 90 × 90 mm** |
| **Size including mortar joint** | **200 × 100 × 100 mm** |

The difference is the **10 mm mortar joint** added on each of the three dimensions. Designing to the 200 × 100 × 100 module is what makes brickwork dimensionally coordinated: a 1 m length takes exactly 5 bricks, and wall thicknesses come out as clean multiples.

The useful consequences:
- One cubic metre of brickwork contains about **500 modular bricks**.
- The ratio 200 : 100 : 100 = **2 : 1 : 1** lets bricks be laid as headers or stretchers in the same course without cutting.
- Traditional (non-modular) bricks of 230 × 110 × 70 mm are still widely made in Nepal and India, which is why option (c) is a plausible distractor — but it is not the *modular* size.

Tolerances under IS 1077 are specified on a batch of 20 bricks rather than individually, since hand-moulded bricks vary.

examTip.trick: The modular brick is **190 × 90 × 90 mm**, and adding a **10 mm mortar joint** on each dimension gives the clean nominal module **200 × 100 × 100**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brick 190, module 200** — the round numbers are the whole point of the modular system. The traditional non-modular brick is 230 × 110 × 70, giving a 240 mm wall instead of 200.

questions.stem: In a tensile test on rebar, the characteristic yield strength of Fe 500 grade steel is:
questions.solution:
**500 N/mm².**

The grade designation *is* the characteristic yield strength in N/mm² — Fe 500 means f_{y} = 500 N/mm². Characteristic strength is defined as the value below which not more than **5%** of test results are expected to fall.

Grades in IS 1786, with the minimum ductility that goes with each:

| Grade | f_{y} (N/mm²) | Minimum elongation |
|---|---|---|
| Fe 250 (mild steel, IS 432) | 250 | 23% |
| Fe 415 | 415 | 14.5% |
| **Fe 500** | **500** | **12%** |
| Fe 550 | 550 | 10% |

Note the trade-off the table shows: as strength rises, **ductility falls**. That is why seismic codes prefer Fe 500D (the D grade has enhanced elongation) over plain Fe 500 — a structure in an earthquake needs to deform without fracturing.

For limit state design the **design** yield strength is the characteristic value divided by the partial safety factor for steel:
> f_{yd} = f_{y}/1.15 = 0.87 f_{y} = 435 N/mm² for Fe 500

The tensile test itself (IS 1608) reports yield stress, ultimate tensile strength and percentage elongation on a gauge length of 5.65√A_{o}.

examTip.trick: The grade number **is** the characteristic yield strength in N/mm². No conversion is needed for Fe250, Fe415, Fe500 or Fe550.
examTip.mnemonic: **The number IS the strength — but the DESIGN strength is 0.87 f_y**, so Fe500 designs at 435 N/mm². The 0.87 is 1/1.15, the partial safety factor for steel.

questions.stem: The centre line method of estimating is most suitable when:
options: The walls of the building are of different thicknesses
Only the foundation is to be estimated
The building has a circular plan only
The walls of the building are of the same thickness throughout
questions.solution:
**When all the walls are of the same thickness.**

In the centre line method the **total centre-line length** of all the walls is measured once, and each item of work is obtained by multiplying that single length by the item's breadth and depth:

> Quantity = total centre line length × breadth × depth

It is quick and involves no separate long-wall/short-wall bookkeeping, but it is only valid while the breadth is the **same** for every wall — otherwise one length cannot serve for all of them.

The crucial refinement: **at every cross junction, deduct half the breadth of the layer for each junction** from the centre line length. Without that deduction the overlapping quantity at the junction is counted twice. (At a simple corner of a rectangular building no deduction is needed, because the two overlaps cancel.)

The alternative method:

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Centre line** | **Walls of uniform thickness**; fast |
| **Long wall–short wall (out-to-out / in-to-in)** | **Walls of differing thickness**; treats each wall separately |

So where a building has, say, 230 mm external and 115 mm internal walls, the long wall–short wall method must be used instead.

examTip.trick: The centre line method uses **one length for every item** in the wall, which only works if the wall's cross section is the same throughout. Different thicknesses need the **long wall–short wall** method instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **One length, many items — but DEDUCT half the breadth at every junction**, for each junction. Forgetting the junction deduction over-measures the work, and is the standard error in this method.

questions.stem: The plasticity index of a soil is defined as:
questions.solution:
**Liquid limit − plastic limit.**

> PI = LL − PL

The plasticity index is the **range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically** — that is, it can be remoulded without cracking or flowing. A wide range means a highly plastic, clay-rich soil.

The Atterberg limits in order of decreasing water content: **liquid limit → plastic limit → shrinkage limit.**

Classification by plasticity index:

| PI | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | Non-plastic (sand) |
| < 7 | Low plasticity |
| 7 – 17 | Medium plasticity |
| > 17 | High plasticity |

The related indices, which the distractors are drawn from:

| Index | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Plasticity index** | **LL − PL** |
| Shrinkage index | PL − SL |
| Liquidity index | (w − PL)/PI |
| Consistency index | (LL − w)/PI |
| Flow index | Slope of the water content vs log N line |
| Toughness index | PI / flow index |

Liquid limit is found with the **Casagrande apparatus** (25 blows to close a 12.7 mm groove) or the cone penetrometer; plastic limit by rolling a 3 mm thread until it just crumbles. PI feeds directly into the **plasticity chart** used for classification in the USCS, where the A-line, PI = 0.73(LL − 20), separates clays from silts.

examTip.trick: **PI = LL − PL** measures the **range of water content over which the soil is plastic** — wide for a fat clay, near zero for a silt.
examTip.mnemonic: **PI = LL − PL.** Its companion is the **liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI**, which locates the *natural* water content within that range: above 1 and the soil behaves as a liquid, which is the condition of a sensitive clay when remoulded.

questions.stem: For a soil with specific gravity 2.65 and void ratio 0.65, the critical hydraulic gradient is:
questions.solution:
**1.00.**

> i_{cr} = (G_{s} − 1)/(1 + e)

**Substituting:**
> i_{cr} = (2.65 − 1)/(1 + 0.65)
> i_{cr} = 1.65/1.65 = **1.00**

The numbers in this question are the standard textbook pair, chosen precisely because they give exactly unity — which is why the critical hydraulic gradient of a typical sand is quoted as **approximately 1**.

**What it means physically.** At i = i_{cr} the upward seepage force per unit volume exactly equals the submerged unit weight of the soil, so

> σ′ = 0

The grains are momentarily weightless, the soil loses all shear strength (τ = σ′ tan φ′ = 0) and it **boils** — the quick sand condition.

**Where it bites in practice:** the downstream toe of an earth dam or weir, and the base of a sheet-piled excavation dewatered from inside. The factor of safety against piping is

> FoS = i_{cr} / i_{actual}

and a value of 4 to 5 is normally required. The remedies are to lengthen the seepage path (cut-off wall, sheet piling, upstream blanket) or to load the exit with an **inverted filter** so that σ′ cannot reach zero.

Note that i_{cr} depends only on G_{s} and e — **not on permeability**, and not on the size of the grains.

examTip.trick: **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) = 1.65/1.65 = 1.00** ✓ — the classic textbook combination, chosen so the answer comes out at exactly 1.
examTip.mnemonic: **i_c ≈ 1 for almost every soil**, because (G − 1) and (1 + e) are usually close. At that gradient the upward seepage force equals the submerged weight, **σ′ = 0**, and the sand has no strength at all — the quick condition.

questions.stem: According to the Mohr–Coulomb theory, the plane of maximum shear stress is inclined to the major principal plane at:
questions.solution:
**45°.**

On the Mohr circle, shear stress is the vertical ordinate, so it is greatest at the **top of the circle**. Since angles on the Mohr circle are **double** the physical angles, the top of the circle sits 90° round from the major principal point — corresponding to a physical plane at **45°** to the major principal plane.

The magnitude there is the radius of the circle:
> τ_{max} = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2

**Do not confuse this with the failure plane.** These are two different planes, and the distinction is examined:

| Plane | Inclination to major principal plane | On Mohr circle |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum shear stress** | **45°** | Top of the circle |
| **Failure plane** | **45° + φ/2** | Point of tangency with the failure envelope |

Failure does **not** occur on the plane of maximum shear (except when φ = 0, as in an undrained clay, where the two coincide at 45°). It occurs on the plane where the ratio of shear to normal stress first reaches the envelope τ = c + σ tan φ — and because normal stress helps resist sliding, that plane is rotated to **45° + φ/2**.

Hence the standard relation at failure:
> σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)

examTip.trap: **45 + φ/2** is the **FAILURE** plane and is the standard confusion. The question asks for the plane of **maximum shear stress**, which is a different plane.
examTip.trick: On Mohr's circle the maximum shear is at the top — **2θ = 90°**, so **θ = 45°** — always, whatever φ. The **failure** plane is where the circle touches the envelope, at **45 + φ/2**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum shear at 45°; failure at 45 + φ/2.** They coincide only when φ = 0. Soil does not fail on the plane of maximum shear, because the normal stress there is higher than on the true failure plane.

questions.stem: For a cohesionless soil with an angle of internal friction of 30°, Rankine's coefficient of active earth pressure is:
questions.solution:
**1/3.**

Rankine's active earth pressure coefficient:

> K_{a} = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45° − φ/2)

**Substituting φ = 30°, so sin 30° = 0.5:**
> K_{a} = (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.5/1.5 = **1/3**

Check by the other form: tan²(45° − 15°) = tan²30° = (0.5774)² = 0.333 ✓

The **passive** coefficient is the reciprocal:
> K_{p} = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = 1.5/0.5 = **3**

which is why option (d) is there — it is K_{p}, not K_{a}. Note K_{p} = 1/K_{a} always, and for φ = 30° the pair 1/3 and 3 is worth memorising outright.

The three states of earth pressure, in increasing order:

| State | Coefficient at φ = 30° | Wall movement |
|---|---|---|
| **Active** | **K_{a} = 1/3** | Wall moves **away** from the soil |
| At rest | K_{o} = 1 − sin φ = 0.5 | No movement |
| Passive | K_{p} = 3 | Wall moves **into** the soil |

The resulting active thrust on a wall of height H is P_{a} = ½K_{a}γH², acting at H/3 above the base.

Rankine's theory assumes a smooth vertical wall and no wall friction; **Coulomb's theory** admits wall friction and a sloping back, and is used where those matter.

examTip.trick: **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 1/3.** For φ = 30° the numbers are exact and worth memorising.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ = 30° gives K_a = 1/3 and K_p = 3, and K_p = 1/K_a.** Check any answer for plausibility: **K_a < 1 < K_p** always. Also **K₀ = 1 − sin φ = 0.5** — halfway between, which is why a restrained basement wall carries about 50% more than an active one.

questions.stem: In Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory, the value of the bearing capacity factor N_{c} for a purely cohesive soil (φ = 0) is:
questions.solution:
**5.7.**

Terzaghi's ultimate bearing capacity for a strip footing:

> q_{u} = cN_{c} + γD_{f}N_{q} + 0.5γBN_{γ}

For a purely cohesive soil, φ = 0, and the factors become
> **N_{c} = 5.7**,  N_{q} = 1.0,  N_{γ} = 0

so the expression collapses to
> q_{u} = 5.7c + γD_{f}

and the **net** ultimate bearing capacity is simply q_{nu} = 5.7c — independent of the footing width, which is a distinctive feature of clay.

Why the distractors are tempting:
- **1.0** is N_{q} at φ = 0, not N_{c}.
- **9.0** is the factor for the **end bearing of a pile** in clay, q_{p} = 9c_{u} — a different problem entirely.
- **17.7** is roughly N_{c} at φ = 20°.

Related points that travel with this:
- Terzaghi's analysis assumes **general shear failure**, a rough footing base, and a shallow footing (D_{f}/B ≤ 1).
- The **safe** bearing capacity is q_{safe} = q_{nu}/FoS + γD_{f}, with FoS usually 2.5 to 3.
- Skempton's and Meyerhof's theories refine N_{c} for footing shape and depth; Meyerhof also allows for inclined loading.
- **Allowable** bearing pressure is the lesser of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure that keeps settlement within permissible limits — in clay, settlement usually governs.

examTip.trick: For **φ = 0** the whole equation collapses: **N_q = 1, N_γ = 0, N_c = 5.7** (Terzaghi) or **5.14** (Prandtl, which IS 6403 uses).
examTip.mnemonic: **5.14 at a shallow strip footing, rising to 9 at a deep pile tip.** Those are two ends of one relationship — N_c grows as the failure surface becomes confined, reaching the pile value at about D/B = 4. Note also that **N_γ = 0 means clay's bearing capacity is independent of footing width**.

questions.stem: The point of contraflexure in a beam is the point where:
questions.solution:
**Bending moment changes sign** (and so passes through zero).

At a point of contraflexure the curvature of the beam reverses — sagging becomes hogging or vice versa — so the bending moment must pass through **zero while changing sign**. The name says exactly that: *contra-flexure*, opposite bending.

The distinctions the distractors are probing:

| Condition | What it locates |
|---|---|
| **BM = 0 and changes sign** | **Point of contraflexure** |
| **SF = 0 (changes sign)** | Point of **maximum bending moment** |
| Slope dy/dx = 0 | Point of **maximum deflection** |

Option (a) is the classic trap: since S = dM/dx, zero **shear** marks the point where the BM diagram is flat, that is a **maximum** moment — not a contraflexure.

Where they occur: only in beams that carry both sagging and hogging moments — **overhanging** beams, **continuous** beams and **fixed** beams. A simply supported beam under downward load sags throughout and has no point of contraflexure at all (except trivially at the supports).

**Practical importance.** The point of contraflexure is where the bending moment is zero, so it is the natural place to **curtail reinforcement** or to locate a **construction joint or splice** — and in a portal frame it is where a hinge may be assumed in approximate analysis.

examTip.trap: "Bending moment is zero" alone is not enough — the moment is zero at both ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not contraflexure points. The moment must **change sign**.
examTip.trick: At contraflexure the beam switches from sagging to hogging, so the **tension face swaps** from bottom to top.
examTip.mnemonic: **It locates where reinforcement can be curtailed** — and it MOVES with the load pattern, so curtail on the envelope of all cases, never on one analysis. It is also the basis of **effective length**: between two contraflexure points a member behaves as a pin-ended strut.

questions.stem: A shaft of diameter d is subjected to a torque T. The maximum shear stress developed is:
questions.solution:
**16T/πd³.**

The torsion equation:

> T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L

so  τ_{max} = T·r/J, with r = d/2 at the surface.

**For a solid circular shaft:**
> J = πd⁴/32
> τ_{max} = T(d/2)/(πd⁴/32) = 32Td/(2πd⁴) = **16T/πd³**

**Dimensional check** — the fastest filter. Stress is force/length², and T is force × length, so T/d³ has the right dimensions while T/d⁴ does not. That alone eliminates options (c) and (d).

Option (b), 32T/πd³, is the common slip — it comes from forgetting the factor of 2 in r = d/2, or from confusing this with the **bending** stress formula for the same section, σ = 32M/πd³.

Worth holding side by side:

| Loading | Maximum stress in a solid circular section |
|---|---|
| **Torsion** | **τ = 16T/πd³** |
| Bending | σ = 32M/πd³ |

For a **hollow** shaft, J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 and τ_{max} = 16TD/[π(D⁴ − d⁴)] — which is why hollow shafts are so efficient: removing the lightly stressed core saves weight while barely reducing J.

Torsional stiffness is GJ/L, and the angle of twist θ = TL/GJ.

examTip.trick: **τ_max = Tr/J = T(d/2)/(πd⁴/32) = 16T/πd³.** Derive it rather than memorise it — the two ingredients are r = d/2 and J = πd⁴/32.
examTip.mnemonic: **Third power for stress, fourth power for stiffness** — exactly parallel to bending's Z = πd³/32 and I = πd⁴/64. Doubling a shaft's diameter multiplies its strength by 8 and its torsional stiffness by 16.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the partial safety factor for concrete and steel in the limit state of collapse are respectively:
questions.solution:
**1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel.**

IS 456 cl. 36.4.2 divides each characteristic material strength by a partial safety factor γ_{m} to obtain the design strength:

| Material | γ_{m} | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Concrete** | **1.5** | 0.67 f_{ck}/1.5 = **0.446 f_{ck}** |
| **Steel** | **1.15** | f_{y}/1.15 = **0.87 f_{y}** |

**Why concrete gets the larger factor:** concrete is mixed, placed and cured on site, so its actual strength scatters far more than that of factory-rolled steel. The 0.67 applied to f_{ck} before dividing is a separate allowance for the difference between cube strength and the strength of concrete in a flexural member under sustained load.

Those two numbers — **0.446 f_{ck}** and **0.87 f_{y}** — appear in every limit state calculation, which is why they are worth memorising in that form rather than as raw safety factors.

The corresponding **load** factors (IS 456 Table 18) for the limit state of collapse:

| Combination | Factor |
|---|---|
| DL + LL | **1.5 (DL + LL)** |
| DL + WL/EL | 1.2 (DL + LL + WL) or 1.5 (DL + WL) |
| DL opposing (overturning, uplift) | **0.9 DL** |

For the limit state of **serviceability** all partial safety factors on materials are taken as **1.0**, which is where option (d) comes from.

examTip.trick: Concrete gets the larger factor because it is **made on site** from variable materials by variable workmanship; steel is **factory-made to specification** and its strength is far more reliable.
examTip.mnemonic: **1.5 concrete, 1.15 steel — hence design strengths of 0.446 f_ck and 0.87 f_y.** The extra 0.67 on concrete accounts for the difference between a laboratory cube and concrete in a real member under sustained load.

questions.stem: For a singly reinforced rectangular beam designed by the limit state method using Fe 415 steel, the limiting depth of the neutral axis is:
questions.solution:
**0.48 d.**

The limiting neutral axis depth is fixed by requiring that the steel reaches its design yield strain at the same time as the concrete reaches its ultimate strain of 0.0035 — the **balanced** condition. Beyond that depth the section would be over-reinforced and would fail by crushing of the concrete without warning.

IS 456 cl. 38.1 gives:

| Steel grade | x_{u,max}/d |
|---|---|
| Fe 250 | **0.53** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** |
| Fe 500 | **0.46** |

The ratio **falls as the grade rises**, because higher-strength steel has a larger yield strain and so needs a shallower neutral axis to reach it while the concrete strain is still 0.0035.

Option (a), 0.42, is a different quantity that sits right next to this one in the same derivation: **0.42 x_{u}** is the depth of the **centroid of the concrete compressive stress block** below the extreme compression fibre. Hence the lever arm z = d − 0.42x_{u}, and the moment of resistance

> M_{u} = 0.87 f_{y} A_{st} (d − 0.42x_{u})

Design practice: keep **x_{u} ≤ x_{u,max}** so the section is **under-reinforced** and fails in a ductile manner, with the steel yielding first and giving visible warning through cracking and deflection.

examTip.trick: **x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002)**. For Fe415 that gives **0.48**; for Fe250 it is 0.53, and for Fe500 it is 0.46.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fe250 → 0.53, Fe415 → 0.48, Fe500 → 0.46 — the limit FALLS as the steel gets stronger.** Its purpose is to force an **under-reinforced (ductile)** section: the steel must yield before the concrete crushes, so failure gives warning. Exceeding it is not permitted at all.

questions.stem: As per IS 800, the minimum pitch of bolts in a connection shall not be less than:
questions.solution:
**2.5 times the nominal bolt diameter.**

IS 800 cl. 10.2.2 sets the **minimum pitch** — the centre-to-centre distance between adjacent bolts along the line of stress — at

> p_{min} = 2.5 d

where d is the nominal diameter of the bolt.

**Why a minimum is needed at all:** bolts placed too close together leave too little metal between the holes, so the plate tears through the net section between them; the bearing zones of adjacent bolts overlap; and there is not enough clearance to swing a spanner or run an impact wrench.

The companion limits, all from cl. 10.2:

| Requirement | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Minimum pitch** | **2.5 d** |
| Maximum pitch | 32 t or 300 mm, whichever is less (t = thinner plate) |
| Minimum edge distance | 1.7 × hole diameter (sheared edge), 1.5 × (rolled/machine-cut edge) |
| Maximum edge distance | 12 t ε, where ε = √(250/f_{y}) |

The maximum pitch exists for a different reason — to stop the plates buckling apart between fasteners and to keep moisture out of the faying surface.

**Gauge** is the corresponding spacing measured *transverse* to the direction of stress; the same 2.5 d minimum applies. **Staggered** bolting increases the net section available and is used where the pitch would otherwise be too tight.

examTip.trick: Two spacing limits, and they exist for opposite reasons: **minimum pitch 2.5d** prevents the bolts from tearing the plate between them and leaves room for the spanner; **maximum pitch** (16t or 200 mm) stops the plates buckling apart between fasteners.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum 2.5d for strength and access; maximum for stability.** Edge distance is separately specified — typically 1.5 times the hole diameter for a rolled edge.

questions.stem: The standard BOD test for sewage is carried out for:
questions.solution:
**5 days at 20°C** — reported as BOD₅.

Biochemical oxygen demand measures the oxygen consumed by micro-organisms while they oxidise the biodegradable organic matter in a sample. Complete oxidation would take about 20 days, which is far too long to be useful, so the test is standardised at **5 days incubation at 20°C**, by which point roughly **68%** of the ultimate BOD has been exerted.

The 20°C figure is chosen as a representative temperature of natural waters in temperate regions. In tropical practice a **3-day test at 27°C** is often used instead, because the reaction runs faster there and gives a comparable fraction of the ultimate demand — which is why option (a) is a plausible distractor rather than a nonsense one.

The first-order relation between the two:
> BOD_{t} = L₀ (1 − 10^{−kt})

with the deoxygenation constant k ≈ 0.1 per day at 20°C, corrected for temperature by k_{T} = k₂₀ (1.047)^{T−20}.

Related measures, constantly compared:

| Parameter | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **BOD** | Biodegradable organics, biologically | 5 days |
| **COD** | Total oxidisable organics, chemically | ~3 hours; always **COD > BOD** |
| ThOD | Theoretical oxygen demand, stoichiometric | Calculated |

The **BOD/COD ratio** indicates biodegradability: above about 0.5 the wastewater is amenable to biological treatment, which is why domestic sewage suits an activated sludge plant while many industrial effluents do not.

Typical raw domestic sewage in Nepal has a BOD₅ of roughly 200–300 mg/L.

examTip.trick: **BOD₅ at 20 °C** is the convention: five days because that is roughly how long a river takes to travel to the sea in the temperate catchments where the test was devised, and 20 °C as a standard temperature.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOD₅ at 20 °C captures only about 68% of the ultimate BOD.** Contrast with **COD**, which oxidises everything chemically in 3 hours — faster and more reproducible, but it includes non-biodegradable matter, so **COD > BOD** always.

questions.stem: If the duty of a crop is 1200 hectares per cumec and the base period is 120 days, the delta is:
questions.solution:
**86.4 cm.**

The standard relation between delta and duty:

> Δ = 8.64 B / D

where Δ is the delta in **metres**, B the base period in **days**, and D the duty in **hectares per cumec**.

**Substituting:**
> Δ = 8.64 × 120 / 1200
> Δ = 1036.8 / 1200 = 0.864 m = **86.4 cm**

**Confirming from first principles.** A discharge of 1 cumec running for the whole base period delivers
> V = 1 × 86 400 × 120 = 1.0368 × 10⁷ m³

and that volume is spread over the area the cumec commands, D = 1200 ha = 1.2 × 10⁷ m²:
> Δ = 1.0368 × 10⁷ / 1.2 × 10⁷ = 0.864 m = **86.4 cm** ✓

**Where the 8.64 comes from:** there are 86 400 seconds in a day and 10 000 m² in a hectare, and 86 400/10 000 = 8.64. The constant therefore already carries the unit conversion, which is why Δ emerges in metres — forgetting that is the commonest source of a factor-of-100 error here.

Note the inverse relationship: a **high duty means a low delta**, since one cumec is irrigating more land and so applying less depth to each hectare.

For reference, typical deltas: rice 100–125 cm, sugarcane 90–100 cm, cotton 50 cm, wheat 40 cm.

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64 B/D** metres, with B in days and D in hectares/cumec. Here: **8.64 × 120/1200 = 0.864 m = 86.4 cm** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **The 8.64 comes from 86 400 seconds in a day ÷ 10 000 m² per hectare.** Note the inverse relationship: **higher duty means LESS water per hectare**, so a high duty is a sign of an *efficient* system, not a thirsty one.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cause of waterlogging?
options: Deep water table and high evaporation
questions.solution:
**A deep water table with high evaporation** — that is the opposite of a waterlogging condition.

Waterlogging is the condition in which the **water table rises so close to the ground surface** that the root zone becomes saturated and the air in the soil pores is displaced. Crops then fail from lack of aeration, and salts are drawn to the surface as the shallow water evaporates.

The genuine causes, all of which raise the water table:
- **Over-irrigation** with inadequate drainage — more water applied than the soil can transmit away.
- **Seepage from unlined canals** and reservoirs, the largest single contributor in many command areas.
- **Obstruction of natural drainage** by roads, railway embankments and canal banks built across drainage lines.
- Flat topography, impervious subsoil, and heavy rainfall.

A **deep** water table with high evaporation is precisely the drained condition that waterlogging destroys, so it cannot be a cause.

**Effects:** poor aeration and root respiration, salinity and alkalinity from capillary rise and evaporation, difficulty in cultivation, weed growth, and a fall in yield.

**Remedies:** line the canals, provide **surface and sub-surface drains** (open ditches or buried perforated pipe), lower the water table by tube wells (vertical drainage), regulate the irrigation supply, and grow crops of high water requirement to draw the table down.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. A **deep** water table and high evaporation are precisely the conditions that **prevent** waterlogging.
examTip.trick: Waterlogging means the water table has risen **into the root zone** — so its causes all involve water arriving faster than it leaves: over-irrigation, canal seepage, poor drainage, impervious subsoil, flat topography.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging is a HIGH water table problem.** Its companion evil is **salinity**: capillary rise brings salts to the surface and evaporation concentrates them there. The remedy for both is **drainage**.

questions.stem: As per the Nepal Road Standard, roads are classified into:
options: National Highway, Feeder Road, District Road and Urban Road
Expressway, National Highway and Village Road
Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Road only
Class I, Class II and Class iii Road
questions.solution:
**National Highway, Feeder Road, District Road and Urban Road.**

The Nepal Road Standard classifies the road network **functionally**, by the role each road plays in the system:

| Class | Function | Designation |
|---|---|---|
| **National Highway** | Main arterial routes running the length and breadth of the country | H (e.g. H01 Mahendra Highway) |
| **Feeder Road** | Connect district headquarters and important economic centres to the highways | F |
| **District Road** | Serve traffic within a district | D |
| **Urban Road** | Roads inside municipal areas | U |
