This is distinct from the Indian (IRC/Nagpur) classification of Expressway, National Highway, State Highway, Major District Road, Other District Road and Village Road — which is what option (b) half-remembers.

Roads are separately classified by **terrain**, which governs the geometric design standards applied: **Plain (up to 10% cross slope), Rolling (10–25%), Mountainous (25–60%) and Steep (over 60%)**. The same functional class carries different design speeds in different terrain — a national highway is designed for 120 km/h in the plains but as little as 40 km/h in steep terrain.

Roads are also described by **surface type** — earthen, gravelled, or blacktopped/bituminous — which is a construction description rather than a classification of function.

examTip.trick: The Nepal Road Standard classifies by **function and administration**, not by pavement type: **National Highway → Feeder Road → District Road → Urban Road**, in descending order of importance.
examTip.mnemonic: **National, Feeder, District, Urban.** The classification determines the design standards, the geometric criteria and — importantly — which agency owns and maintains the road.

questions.stem: The stopping sight distance for a vehicle consists of:
questions.solution:
**Lag distance plus braking distance.**

> SSD = lag distance + braking distance = **vt + v²/(2gf)**

where v is the design speed in m/s, t the total reaction time (taken as **2.5 s** by IRC), g = 9.81 m/s² and f the longitudinal coefficient of friction.

The two parts are physically distinct:
- **Lag distance** — the distance covered while the driver *perceives* the hazard and *reacts*, before the brakes are applied at all. Nothing is decelerating during this time, so it is simply v × t.
- **Braking distance** — the distance covered once the brakes are on, obtained by equating kinetic energy to the work done against friction: ½mv² = f·mg·s, giving s = v²/(2gf).

On a **gradient** the friction term is modified, since gravity helps or hinders:
> SSD = vt + v²/[2g(f ± 0.01n)]

with + for an ascending and − for a descending gradient — so the required sight distance is **longer downhill**, which is the case that governs design.

The values of f fall with speed: 0.40 at 20–30 km/h down to 0.35 at 100 km/h.

The other sight distances, for contrast:

| Sight distance | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **SSD** | Stop safely — the absolute minimum, provided everywhere |
| **OSD** | Overtake safely on a two-lane two-way road; ≈ 14.4 v (v in km/h) |
| ISD | See across an intersection |

On a **two-way single-lane** road the sight distance provided must be **twice** the SSD, since both vehicles must stop — the grain of truth that option (d) distorts.

examTip.trick: **SSD = lag distance + braking distance**. The lag distance is what the vehicle travels during the driver's **reaction time** (taken as 2.5 s); the braking distance is v²/(2gf).
examTip.mnemonic: **SSD = vt + v²/(2gf).** Both terms matter, and the reaction term dominates at low speeds. Related distances: **overtaking sight distance** is far longer, and **intermediate sight distance = 2 × SSD**.

questions.stem: In a flexible pavement, the wheel load is transferred to the subgrade:
options: Through grain-to-grain contact, over a wide area
Entirely by the flexural strength of the top layer
As a concentrated load at a single point
questions.solution:
**Through grain-to-grain contact, spreading the load over a wide area.**

A flexible pavement is a **layered** system with no significant flexural strength of its own. Each layer transmits the wheel load to the one below by **grain-to-grain contact**, so the stressed area widens with depth in a roughly conical distribution. By the time the load reaches the subgrade it is spread over a large enough area for the pressure to fall within what the soil can carry.

The consequences follow directly:
- Layers are arranged in **decreasing order of strength** downward — bituminous surfacing, base course, sub-base, subgrade — because the stress reduces with depth.
- Thickness design is governed by the **subgrade strength**, measured by the **CBR** test, using IRC 37 or the DoR guidelines. A weak subgrade needs a thicker pavement.
- The pavement **deflects** under load and recovers; its surface reflects any settlement of the subgrade beneath.

Contrast with a **rigid** pavement:

| | Flexible | Rigid |
|---|---|---|
| Load transfer | **Grain-to-grain, layer by layer** | **Slab action — flexural strength** |
| Design basis | Subgrade CBR | Modulus of subgrade reaction k, Westergaard analysis |
| Critical stress | Vertical compressive stress on subgrade | Flexural (tensile) stress in the slab |
| Joints | None | Contraction, expansion and warping joints |
| Behaviour on weak subgrade | Reflects settlement | Bridges over local weakness |

Option (b) describes the rigid pavement, and is the intended trap.

examTip.trick: A **flexible** pavement has no bending strength of its own, so the load spreads downward through successive layers by **grain-to-grain contact**, arriving at the subgrade over a wide area at low intensity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flexible spreads through the layers; RIGID bridges over in FLEXURE as a slab.** That is why a rigid pavement can span a soft patch and a flexible one cannot — and why the two are designed by completely different methods (CBR and layer thickness against slab flexural stress).

questions.stem: In an isometric projection, the three principal axes are inclined to each other at:
questions.solution:
**120°.**

In isometric projection the object is oriented so that all three mutually perpendicular edges make equal angles with the plane of projection. Their projections therefore divide the circle equally, and the three isometric axes sit at **120° to one another** — conventionally drawn as one vertical axis and two at 30° above the horizontal on either side.

The word itself says so: *iso-metric*, equal measure.

The consequences worth knowing:
- Because the edges are inclined to the plane, they project **shorter than true length** — the true ratio is **0.816**, the **isometric scale**.
- An **isometric drawing** (as distinct from an isometric *projection*) is drawn with true lengths for convenience, so it comes out about **1.22 times larger** than the strict projection, while looking identical in shape.
- A circle on any isometric face projects as an **ellipse**, drawn by the four-centre method.

The family of pictorial projections:

| Projection | Angles between axes | Foreshortening |
|---|---|---|
| **Isometric** | **All 120°** | All three axes equally |
| Dimetric | Two equal | Two axes equally |
| Trimetric | All different | All three differently |
| Oblique / cabinet | Front face true shape | Depth axis only |

Contrast **orthographic** projection, where the object faces are parallel to the projection planes and each view — plan, elevation, end view — shows true shape but only two dimensions at a time. Isometric shows all three dimensions in a single view, which is why it is used for pictorial and assembly drawings.

examTip.trick: The three isometric axes are equally inclined, so they divide 360° into three equal parts: **360/3 = 120°**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Isometric = EQUAL measure — 120° apart, and all three axes scaled identically.** The isometric scale is about **0.816** of true length, though most drawings use full-size lengths for convenience and accept the slight enlargement.
